text:
By: CATHERINE WATKINS, Hydrocarbon Processing

Hydrogen's (H2’s) reality check: the money is flowing, the offtake isn't. At the 16th Dii Desert Energy Leadership Summit in Istanbul, producers, engineers, buyers and shippers agreed that hydrogen technology is ready, but the bottleneck is bankable demand, and the first real market may be the refinery.

Five years ago, H2 panels were about ambition. Now, the "Hydrogen Reality Check" session at Dii Desert Energy's summit was about execution. Chaired by Dan Feldman, Global Head of Energy at King & Spalding, the discussion brought together Air Products Qudra, Masdar, thyssenkrupp Uhde, Smartenergy, SEFE, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Fraunhofer ISE. Their shared verdict: the sector has moved from announcing gigawatts to financing them, and the hard part now is commercial, not technical.

The money is real. Dr. Faye Al Hersh, Associate Director, Development UAE at Masdar, anchored the discussion in the Hydrogen Council's new Global Hydrogen Compass 2026. Committed clean H2 investments have reached $130 B, with 6.9 MMtpy of capacity across more than 570 projects that have passed final investment decision (FID). Operating capacity grew 70% in a year to approximately 1.7 MMtpy.

The drivers are shifting too. The Compass finds that energy security, resilience and industrial growth now match or exceed decarbonization as the main rationale in most regions with committed investment.

The host country was candid about the pace. Opening the summit, YEO Technology Chairman and CEO Tolunay Yıldız said H2 progress has been slower than many hoped: costs remain high, and buyers and investors need regulatory frameworks and long-term commitments. He still backed green H2 for hard-to-electrify industries and pointed to Turkey’s target of 5 GW of electrolyzer capacity by 2035.

Bankability is the bottleneck. Fatemah Din, Senior Vice President MENA at thyssenkrupp Uhde, put it plainly: the challenge is no longer the technology. It is bankability, long-term offtake agreements and stable regulation. What the market needs now, she argued, is success stories measured not in gigawatts announced but in FIDs reached, gigawatts contracted and infrastructure built.

Al Hersh described the mismatch at the heart of the problem. Buyers of ammonia, methanol and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) are used to small, short-term contracts, while lenders want long-term offtake before they finance a renewable power plant. Mandates help only when they bite: without penalties, a mandate simply sets the price of non-compliance. She added that EU rules are being transposed unevenly by member states, with refining emerging as the first-mover sector, with wider industry lagging.

Sebastian Budischin, Senior Vice President Business Development at SEFE, spoke from the middle of the value chain. “Producers approach SEFE as the natural offtaker,” he said, “but its own industrial customers struggle to commit long term amid volatile markets and shifting rules. No single company can carry the full market risk of a 10-plus-yr contract for 100,000 tpy, so risk has to be shared along the whole chain.” He warned that if everyone waits for someone else to move first, the industry will be having the same conversation in a few years.

Christian Pho Duc, CTO of Smartenergy, added that H2 only works as part of a wider system of flexibility, storage and gas-grid links, and that offtake demand is strongest where regulation creates a clear obligation.

Follow the refiners, and the pipes. Ebubekir Koyuncu, CEO of Blue Hydrogen Industrial Gases (BHIG) and CEO of Air Products Qudra, offered the most pragmatic view. Market conditions have changed since the industry's early giga-scale bets, and Air Products has adapted by looking for partners and "low-hanging fruit." With refiners earning strong margins, the near-term business is supplying refinery and industrial gas customers, including through what he described as a major H2 pipeline network under construction in the Middle East. “Offtakers,” he said, “remain overwhelmingly price-driven: without mandates or penalties, few will pay a premium for green molecules.”

That puts infrastructure center stage. Panelists agreed that common-user infrastructure (CUI), meaning shared pipelines, storage and export terminals, can de-risk giga-scale projects that no single developer could justify alone. Al Hersh said Masdar's early projects rely on existing infrastructure and pointed to Egypt and Morocco as markets where government-led infrastructure models are taking hold. See urged that shared infrastructure be treated as an enabler, not left to become the bottleneck. She also noted that cheaper solar and batteries are raising electrolyzer utilization and improving project economics.

On carriers, MENA Hydrogen Alliance Chairman Frank Wouters interviewed Eiichiro Miyazoe, Managing Director of Kawasaki Heavy Industries Middle East. Kawasaki is scaling up from the 1,250-m³ Suiso Frontier, the world's first liquefied H2 (LH2) carrier, to a 40,000-m³ vessel ordered by Japan Suiso Energy for demonstration by FY2030. Its boil-off gas will fuel a H2 dual-fuel generator. Kawasaki is also working with EcoLog on an LH2 import terminal at the Port of Amsterdam. Wouters argued that LH2 is often undervalued: liquefaction energy is spent where power is cheap, no cracking is needed at the destination, and large liquefiers are far more efficient than today's small units.

A silk road for eSAF. Wouters also presented the work of Dii's eFuels task force, making the case for Türkiye as a "Silk Road" for SAF. The ingredients are there: a global aviation hub, a national airline operating > 500 aircraft, a 120-GW solar and wind target he expects to be exceeded, and a H2 strategy targeting production costs below $2.40/kg by 2035. Because aircraft bought today will fly for decades, drop-in fuels are one of the few levers aviation has.

He outlined three proven routes:

Power-to-liquid via Fischer-Tropsch

Methanol-to-jet (with methanol made where power is cheap and upgraded in refineries)

HEFA from used cooking oil.

Demand signals are stacking up, from ReFuelEU's requirement of 70% SAF by 2050, including 35% synthetic fuel, to ICAO's CORSIA from Jan. 1, 2027. Türkiye's existing refineries with jet capacity are an asset. The task force's asks to policymakers include early-mover protection against rule changes, more flexibility on CO₂ sourcing until direct air capture matures and multipliers in support schemes.

The long view. Prof. Dr. Christopher Hebling, Director International at Fraunhofer ISE, closed the session with perspective. He showed a 1912 newspaper article warning that coal burning could warm the climate "in a few centuries." The science was right, he noted, but the timing was not: the effects are being felt now, with global emissions approaching 40 Gt of CO₂/yr. Energy transitions have historically been additive, and fossil fuels still supply roughly 80% of primary energy. Even so, solar deployment is now measured in hundreds of gigawatts a year, and research into natural hydrogen and negative emissions is opening new options.

Hebling ended where the panel began: no one succeeds alone. He credited Dii's summit as the kind of platform where research, industry, policy and finance meet and new projects are formed. On the evidence of this session, hydrogen's next chapter will be written less by technology breakthroughs than by who agrees to share the risk.

H2Tech is a supporting partner of the 16th Dii Desert Energy Leadership Summit.

text:
NORMAL, Ill. — Tight margins, rising input costs, shifts in global trading and changing biofuels are all impacting U.S. corn growers.

“These four things are not separate stories — they are all connected,” said Krista Swanson, chief economist for the National Corn Growers Association.

“The U.S. Department of Agriculture shows the net farm cash income for 2026 is expected to land at the 20-year average,” she said during a presentation at the Generations of Women in Agriculture Across America event, a project of the Illinois Agri-Women.

“You would expect 20 years of experience, effort and hard work to show up in your earnings, but it does not work that way on a farm.

“Farms have been getting bigger, machinery is getting more sophisticated, the cost to cash flow a farm has increased a lot and the amount of risk it takes to capitalize that farm has also increased.

“So, we have more acres, risk, machinery and management for the same real return. That is the situation farmers are in right now.”

However, there is a huge deviation around the average depending on various factors such as how much land a farmer owns or rents.

“When you buy your fertilizer can make a big difference or how you market your crop, so some farms are feeling the pressure more than others,” Swanson said.

Fertilizer makes up about 30% to 40% of operating costs for corn growers, the economist said.

“There have been a few years in the past five years where buying fertilizer in the fall versus in the spring has made a really big difference in the overall farm budget,” she said.

The United States produces about 90% of the nitrogen products that farmers apply to their land.

Therefore, Swanson said, farmers were questioning why there were huge spikes in fertilizer prices when the Strait of Hormuz was closed.

“Fertilizers like other agricultural commodities are global commodities,” she said. “If I am a buyer of fertilizer from another part of the world and I normally buy it from the Middle Eastern region, now there is a conflict and a huge jump in price, I am going to buy it from the U.S.

“The reason our prices spiked, even though we are producing it here, is it had to increase to keep the fertilizer here. Otherwise, it would go to other places in the world, so there are a lot of dynamics happening that can be difficult to understand.”

Earlier this summer, NCGA released a study that looked at the cost U.S. farmers pay for inputs compared to farmers in Brazil.

“We partnered with a global research firm and they used data points from thousands of farmers in both countries,” Swanson said.

“Making comparisons across two countries is difficult because the pest pressures are not the same, products that are used are not always exactly the same, the regulatory and tax structure is different and the farm sizes and market structure is different,” she said.

“When we stripped out all the differences possible, we found that U.S. corn and soybean producers pay substantially more than the Brazilian price for seed and crop protection products — and sometimes even more than double.”

One of the exciting things for corn producers is exports, Swanson said.

“We are exporting over 3 billion bushels of corn right now, which is impressive,” she said. “This is a really good thing, because last year we produced a record 17-billion-bushel corn crop.”

However, the U.S. market share of corn exports in terms of volume has changed significantly.

“In 1990, the U.S. had 75% of the global market share, Argentina had 7%, Ukraine had 1%, the rest of the world had 17% and Brazil was not even in the picture,” the economist said.

For the upcoming marketing year, she said, the U.S. market share is expected to be 40% of the global corn exports, with Brazil at 21%, Argentina at 18%, Ukraine at 10% and the rest of the world at 11%.

“That shows the growing competitiveness of Brazil in the global market,” Swanson said.

“For many years U.S. agriculture has been competitive globally because we are the most productive and efficient producers of commodities like corn,” she said.

“The 17-billion-bushel corn crop we produced in 2025 is seven times larger than what we produced in 1925 on fewer planted acres, but the problem is that productivity is not translating to profitability right now.”

Ethanol has been an important driver for corn demand.

“As we look ahead to the coming decade, the amount of motor gasoline we expect to use is declining,” Swanson said.

“Securing year-around, nationwide E15, I believe can make a difference in the short term,” she said. “But as we think longer term, even a higher percentage share of an overall declining market share is still declining in the long run.”

Therefore, the NCGA is doing a lot of work to think about ethanol beyond on road use.

“If corn-based ethanol could capture 10% of the global maritime fuel market, that would be 3 billion bushels of corn per year,” Swanson said.

“If we can capture 10% of the sustainable aviation fuel market, that would be 5 billion bushels of corn per year,” she said. “And if we can capture 10% of the bioeconomy product market, that would be over 6 billion bushels of corn per year.”

So many products that people use and wear have petroleum in them, that include things like plastic water bottles and activewear, which could be replaced with corn-based ethanol.

“This is not an abstract idea,” Swanson stressed. “I have tights made from corn-based ethanol from corn grown in Iowa.”

There are products in the works, but it will take innovation and policy changes to move them to large scale production.

“This is where we need a lot of people advocating and working with Congress to get an environment established where these things can grow,” Swanson said. “Because it can make a big difference.”

text:
France has moved to implement green hydrogen quotas in transport, after proposing a new framework included in the country’s 2027 finance bill, as well as double-sided auctions for e-fuels and further subsidies for hydrogen production.

Designed to implement the EU’s Renewable Energy Directive (RED) III transport mandates, the proposed IRICC will replace the existing TIRUERT framework and impose new carbon intensity reduction obligations.

For hydrogen producers, the mechanism could open demand from refineries and transport applications, helping to provide offtake signals that have remained a barrier to project development across Europe.

While the bill doesn’t specify IRICC requirements, previous consultation documents showed hydrogen quotas of 0.2% from 2027 and 1.5% from 2030.

Trade group France Hydrogène claimed the measure was expected to “trigger” almost €2bn ($2.25bn) in private hydrogen project investment across refining, marine synthetic fuels, and road mobility, dependent on final quota design.

The bill also included plans to introduce a dual-auction mechanism to support green hydrogen-based sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) projects.

It would see the government “guarantee” up to 160,000 tonnes of e-SAF production per year to achieve the country’s 2032 ReFuelEU synthetic fuel obligation of 2%.

The document also confirmed a €1.2bn ($1.35bn) budget for its competitive electrolytic hydrogen project tender, which awarded €778m ($874m) to three projects in its first round.

The scheme provides per-kilogramme subsidies for 15 years, under its wider €4bn ($4.5bn) production incentive programme.

“The French hydrogen sector is at a pivotal moment, needing to make crucial final investment decisions in 2027,” said Nicolas Brahy, President of France Hydrogène. “If these measures are adopted, France’s potential will finally translate into industrial investments.”

The bill will now go through the National Assembly and Senate, with the first formal vote expected on 20 October.

Passage is far from automatic. France’s previous two budgets were ultimately forced through using a constitutional provision after governments struggled to secure parliamentary majorities. The 2026 budget was only finally adopted in February following no-confidence votes.

With France also heading towards a presidential election in 2027, the hydrogen provisions therefore remain subject to political negotiation.

text:
British Airways changed its loyalty programme fundamentally in 2025.

The Executive Club became The British Airways Club, and status now depends mostly on how much you spend rather than how far you fly.

For anyone chasing Bronze, Silver or Gold, the rules have changed again from April 2026.

This guide explains how British Airways tier points work today, how to earn them and how to plan your year.

What Changed at British Airways?

The biggest shift was the move to revenue based status.

Head for Points explains that tier points are now based on spending rather than distance or travel class.

Travel Smarter notes that the Executive Club was rebranded as The British Airways Club in April 2025, with existing membership numbers, Avios balances and status carried over.

Under the old system, a cheap business class ticket to a distant city could earn a lot of tier points.

That approach, known as tier point running, has largely disappeared under the new model.

The Status Thresholds

The tiers remain familiar.

Reward Flight Finder confirms that Bronze requires 3,500 tier points or 25 eligible the airline flights, Silver requires 7,500 tier points or 50 eligible flights, and Gold requires 20,000 tier points.

The flight count route is an important alternative.

Frequent short haul travellers who fly often on cheaper fares can still reach Bronze or Silver without spending large sums.

At the very top is Gold Guest List.

Max Your Trip notes that it requires 65,000 tier points, of which 52,000 must be earned flying on British Airways.

Head for Points adds that renewal requires 40,000 tier points, with at least 32,000 from BA marketed flights and holidays.

How British Airways Tier Points Are Earned

The base rule is simple. Reward Flight Finder explains that on British Airways marketed flights, you earn one tier point per £1 of eligible fare and carrier imposed charges.

Government taxes do not count, although carrier imposed charges do.

Reward Flight Finder gives the example of a Club Europe return to Berlin costing £500 before taxes, which would earn around 500 tier points.

Since 1 April 2026, flights also earn fixed bonus tier points.

Head for Points lists ranges per segment, from 75 to 275 for short haul economy up to 500 to 1,100 for long haul business and 650 to 1,250 for First.

The bonus depends on the route, cabin and fare type.

Flexible fares and premium cabins earn the highest bonuses, which rewards the most valuable customers.

Extras That Earn Tier Points

Ancillary spending now counts too. Head for Points notes that from April 2026, you earn two tier points for every £1 spent on extra baggage or seat selection.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel contributions are another route.

Reward Flight Finder notes that eligible SAF contributions also earn two tier points per £1, capped at 2,000 tier points per collection year.

British Airways Holidays bookings earn tier points as well.

Head for Points explains that where a fare is not disclosed, such as in a flight and hotel package, tier points are based on cabin, booking class and a percentage of miles flown.

Partner Airlines

Partner flights work differently.

The Points Guy explains that flights marketed by most partners earn tier points based on a percentage of miles flown, cabin and booking class.

American Airlines and Iberia marketed flights are treated differently.

Reward Flight Finder notes that these receive fixed extra tier points based on haul and cabin.

For travellers who fly mostly on oneworld partners, this distance based approach can still be valuable.

It is one of the few areas where the old style of earning survives.

Bonus Avios Milestones

The programme also rewards progress within the year.

Head for Points lists bonus Avios at 5,500, 11,000 and 16,000 tier points, worth 2,500, 4,000 and 5,000 Avios respectively.

These milestones encourage members to consolidate their spending with the airline rather than spreading it across rival airlines.

The Membership Year

Timing matters. Max Your Trip explains that the membership year runs from 1 April to 31 March, and status is based on tier points collected within that year.

Travel Smarter notes that tier points reset to zero on 1 April.

Any planning for status therefore needs to be completed before the end of March.

Tier points on a booking are split equally among passengers.

Max Your Trip notes that only travellers who add their British Airways Club number receive the credit.

Lifetime Gold

Lifetime Gold remains available but is now tied to spending.

Head for Points reports that it requires 550,000 tier points, equivalent to £550,000 of net British Airways spend, with existing tier points converted on a pro rata basis.

How to Plan Your Year With British Airways

Start by deciding which route suits you.

Frequent short haul travellers may find the flight count option easier, while long haul and premium travellers will benefit most from the revenue model.

Consolidate your spending.

Paying for seats and bags through BA now earns double tier points, so these add ons contribute more than before.

Track your progress against the milestones.

Hitting 5,500, 11,000 or 16,000 tier points brings bonus Avios, which add value even if you fall short of the next status level.

What Each Tier Unlocks Across oneworld

Status also carries weight beyond British Airways.

The Points Guy notes that Bronze status is equivalent to oneworld Ruby, and higher tiers map to more valuable alliance levels.

Silver corresponds to oneworld Sapphire, which brings business lounge access when flying with oneworld airlines.

Gold corresponds to oneworld Emerald, which adds first class lounge access and fast track security at many airports.

That alliance recognition makes status especially useful for travellers who regularly fly with partners such as American Airlines, Iberia, Qatar Airways or Cathay Pacific.

Is British Airways Status Still Worth It?

For frequent travellers based at Heathrow, the answer is often yes.

Status brings lounge access, priority boarding, extra baggage and better seat selection.

However, the revenue model favours higher spenders.

Travellers who previously earned Silver on cheap long haul fares may find it much harder under the new system.

You can explore the British Airways fleet and network using our Airline Search tool.

The Bottom Line

The British Airways Club rewards spending, not distance.

Understanding how base tier points, fixed bonuses and ancillary earning combine is the key to reaching the status you want.

Plan around the April to March year, use the flight count route if it suits you, and make every pound count.

Airbus Sells Sepang Aircraft Engineering (SAE) MRO to Malaysia Aviation Group

AeroMorning — John Smith — October 1, 2026

On October 1, 2026, Malaysia Aviation Group (MAG)—the parent company of Malaysia Airlines—announced that it had signed a Sale and Purchase Agreement to acquire Airbus’ wholly owned Malaysian Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul (MRO) subsidiary, Sepang Aircraft Engineering (SAE). The undisclosed transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals, including Malaysia’s Civil Aviation Authority, with completion targeted for 2027. MAG stated that the acquisition will strengthen its engineering and maintenance capabilities, broaden its aviation-services portfolio, and accelerate third-party revenue growth.

1. Origins and Evolution under Airbus

Establishment: SAE was founded in 2007 as an independent MRO centre at Kuala Lumpur International Airport, initially servicing Airbus A320 and Boeing 737 aircraft. Airbus acquired a 40% stake and operational control in 2011, followed by the remaining shares in 2017, making SAE a wholly owned subsidiary.

Strategic Role: SAE became part of Airbus’ “Services by Airbus” growth strategy to expand customer services in the rapidly growing Asia-Pacific market. In 2017, Airbus expanded SAE with a second hangar, bringing total floor space to approximately 50,000 square metres, after the facility had already completed 500 C-checks. SAE also supported Malaysia’s A400M fleet and hosted a regional Airbus spare-parts inventory.

Further Investments: In 2019, Airbus announced a further expansion of SAE as part of three initiatives to strengthen its industrial footprint in Malaysia, highlighting the country as one of its most important Asian markets.

SAE is now an established regional MRO business with strong third-party demand in a competitive Asian market:

Recent Deals:

Aircalin: Completed an A320neo C-check at SAE in 2025.

Air India Express: SAE supported two A320 aircraft in 2026.

Cebu Pacific Air: Secured a recent 12-year agreement covering maintenance and end-of-lease checks for seven A320 aircraft, building on a broader relationship covering heavy maintenance, engine changes, structural repairs, and engineering support.

VietJet Air: Secured recent A320-family MRO contracts over the past 12 months.

2. Perspective

Operating in a fiercely competitive Asian MRO landscape where scale is critical, Airbus’ exit comes at a time when SAE has reached sufficient maturity to support MAG’s strategic expansion. Because Malaysia Airlines does not operate the A320, acquiring SAE allows MAG to capture a major customer segment far beyond its own fleet, integrating A320 expertise, a dedicated paint hangar, and specialised component-repair capabilities into its existing MRO activities through MAB Engineering Services.

South African energy and chemicals company Sasol will supply its technology to Project Wigeon, a sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) plant under development in the United States. Dutch project developer SkyNRG announced the agreement on Monday, September 28.

The agreement marks the third project announced since July in which Sasol and Topsoe will jointly provide their technologies. The new contract comes as the two companies prepare to dissolve Zaffra, their joint venture established to develop, build and operate sustainable aviation fuel projects.

Project Wigeon will be built at the Port of Walla Walla in Washington State. The facility aims to produce 50 million U.S. gallons of sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel annually, equivalent to approximately 189 million liters. The developers expect the plant to begin production around 2031.

Sasol will provide its Sasol LTFT™ low-temperature Fischer-Tropsch technology, which converts synthesis gas into liquid hydrocarbons that can be refined into aviation fuel. Meanwhile, Topsoe will supply the technologies required to produce the synthesis gas and upgrade the resulting fuel.

In addition, Sasol and Topsoe have each signed engineering contracts with SkyNRG covering their technologies, engineering design and technical support. Technip Energies is conducting front-end engineering studies to refine the project's design, costs and execution plan.

Sasol Adds New Projects After Announcing Zaffra's Wind-Down

The SkyNRG agreement follows two other contracts signed since July.

The first involves Sustaero, a Canadian company developing a sustainable aviation fuel plant that will use wood waste as feedstock. The project aims to produce 144,000 metric tons of SAF annually during its initial phase. The partners expect a final investment decision in 2027.

The second involves Allied Biofuels, which is developing a sustainable aviation fuel and e-SAF production platform in Uzbekistan. Sasol and Topsoe will provide the project's core technologies, while Allied Biofuels targets a final investment decision in the first quarter of 2027.

These announcements follow the companies' decision to dissolve Zaffra. On June 26, Sasol and Topsoe announced plans to begin the operational wind-down of their joint venture dedicated to developing sustainable aviation fuel projects.

However, the planned dissolution of Zaffra will not end the companies' technology partnership. In June, Sasol and Topsoe said they would continue working together under their 2019 technology licensing agreement.

The licensing framework allows both companies to jointly market their technologies to project developers and customers. The partners had already signed six technology licenses under the agreement when they announced the Zaffra wind-down. Meanwhile, Project Wigeon has entered the front-end engineering and design (FEED) phase, during which engineers refine the project's technical design, cost estimates and execution strategy before a final investment decision.

São Paulo [Brazil], October 2 (ANI): Brazil’s ethanol sector is entering a new phase as emerging technologies in agriculture, aviation and maritime transport are expected to drive demand for the biofuel beyond conventional sugarcane-powered vehicles, according to Henrique Berbert de Amorim Neto, president of the Local Productive Arrangement for Alcohol (APLA).Speaking to Brasil 247 during the Global Agribusiness Forum (GAFFFF) in São Paulo, Amorim said agricultural machinery powered by ethanol could become a major source of new demand.He noted that manufacturers are developing ethanol-powered tractors and sugarcane harvesters, while other technologies are exploring flex-fuel systems capable of incorporating ethanol into diesel engines.Amorim said these developments are converging around the use of ethanol to reduce carbon emissions.

APLA is working with ApexBrasil to promote Brazilian sugar, ethanol and energy technologies in international markets, including countries with existing or potential sugarcane and corn production.Amorim pointed to growing opportunities in Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and marine bunker fuel.He said ethanol-based solutions could contribute to decarbonising maritime transport, while demand from the aviation sector could require a substantial expansion of ethanol production.Brazil’s production capacity, he said, will need to grow significantly to meet emerging demand.
Corn ethanol is currently emerging as the main frontier for this expansion.Amorim said corn-based production has grown rapidly and could account for nearly 30 per cent of Brazil’s ethanol output this year, compared with about 25 per cent last year, as reported by Brasil 247.The shift highlights the diversification of Brazil’s ethanol industry, which has expanded considerably since the launch of the Proálcool programme in 1975, with ethanol production now extending beyond its traditional dependence on sugarcane.

text:
Harjeet Singh is the global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. Julie-Anne Richards is strategic campaign lead for the Make Big Polluters Pay campaign in Australia.

This year, a glacier collapse in Nepal's Himalayan valleys swept away the lives of at least 1,500 people, with recovery costs of US$5 billion, or 10% of national GDP. But this was not a tragedy for which no one can be blamed. This was a crime with a balance sheet - one whose costs are paid by people who did nothing to cause it, and whose profits are booked by polluting corporations that did everything.

Across the Pacific, the calculation of injustice is now brutally clear. According to Oxfam Australia, the average yearly GDP loss of Pacific countries from climate disasters has increased four-fold over the last decade, reaching 14.3% of GDP. The number of Pacific people battered by climate disasters has risen by 700% in a decade. Whole villages are being packed up and moved as the sea takes the land beneath them.

Let's look at the other ledger. This year, as climate change and an oil shock drove up the cost of living for ordinary families, Woodside - touted as “one of Australia's biggest winners” from the war in the Middle East - reported revenues jumping nearly 30% to AUD$6 billion in just three months.

In Australia, Oxfam finds that in 2023-2024, fossil fuel corporations paid only AUD$22.8 billion in corporate income tax - just 5% of their AUD$436 billion in total reported income - while 26 out of 80, or one in every three large fossil fuel corporations, did not pay corporate income tax at all.

The polluters are not struggling to pay for the damage they cause. They are choosing not to.

This is the moral obscenity at the heart of the climate crisis: the money exists. It is simply flowing in the wrong direction. And nowhere is that clearer than in the funds the world built to protect the vulnerable, now left to languish.

Funds struggle to fill their coffers

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has received US$2.8 billion in requests from 119 countries. And Nepal has sought an urgent US$20 million for immediate needs. Yet the Fund has only US$342 million in total to give.

The Pacific Resilience Facility - a fund the Pacific designed for itself, to prepare its own communities - sits well short of even its modest US$500 million capitalisation target. And the Adaptation Fund is running on empty. While adaptation needs in developing countries could reach US$387 billion a year by 2030, according to the latest UNEP Adaptation Gap report, the Fund's resource mobilisation target of a modest US$300 million for 2025 fell far short, with only US$135 million pledged.

This is a matter of priorities, not of resources. For decades, the world has accepted a simple principle - the polluter pays principle - whether through the OECD, of which Australia is a member, or Europe's carbon pricing. New York and Vermont have already passed laws to make Big Oil pay into climate superfunds, and ten more US states are moving to follow.

The idea is neither radical nor new. It's time to make big polluters pay.

Comment: After Hormuz, Nepal and wildfires, people want action to make polluters pay

What is urgently needed is the courage to apply it to the fossil fuel corporations that have spent decades avoiding it. In November, Australia takes up the presidency of the COP31 negotiations, committing to stand shoulder to shoulder with its Pacific neighbours.

Australia, together with the Turkish COP31 Presidency, must guide and inspire progress at the upcoming climate conference, including on new climate finance pledges by developed countries (which agreed to mobilise at least $300 billion by 2035) and triple the funds available to the FRLD, the Adaptation Fund and the other UN climate funds.

Rich countries agreed to these goals two years ago at COP29. Yet, the reality is that developing countries' need for climate finance is in the trillions annually, while developed countries continue to delay providing even what they have already committed. A clear signal recognising the importance of delivering the promised climate finance must come at next week's Pre-COP in the Pacific, and COP31 in Antalya must go on to deliver against existing promises or risk an irreparable breakdown in trust.

Time for a climate pollution levy

Countries must also ensure funding for loss and damage takes its rightful place as the third pillar of climate finance, alongside mitigation and adaptation, in negotiations regarding the UNFCCC climate finance work programme and Article 9 on shifting finance flows towards a low-carbon, resilient world.

Australia, as President of Negotiations and as a Pacific nation, cannot ask the world to fill these funds while it lets its own coal and gas giants off the hook. Australia should not only stop approving new and expanded coal and gas mines, it should also introduce a Climate Pollution Levy on big coal, oil and gas corporations - a charge on every tonne of carbon pollution they extract and profit from. Independent analysis shows such a levy could raise tens of billions of dollars a year, and can be designed so the cost falls on the corporations, not on households.

This is not charity - it is compensation. It is the beginning of accountability. And the public is far ahead of its leaders: eight in 10 people worldwide, and a clear majority of Australians, want fossil fuel firms taxed to pay for the damage they cause.

Fossil fuel expansion threatens COP31 hosts’ credibility, experts warn

The money must go where the harm lands. A Climate Pollution Levy should feed the funds frontline communities are relying on - fully capitalising the Pacific Resilience Facility this year, replenishing the Adaptation Fund, and delivering the billions the loss and damage fund needs.

It is essential for these funds to be able to provide grant-based finance that reaches communities directly, not more loans that push drowning nations deeper into debt. With Nepal’s recovery costs estimated at around 10% of the country's GDP, if we leave it to fend for itself without loss and damage funding, Nepal will likely be saddled with debt and could fail to recover adequately, increasing poverty and inequality.

We have heard enough empty pledges. We have watched enough funds announced with fanfare, only then to be starved in silence. The era of asking polluters politely is over. Australia, as COP31 president, has a rare chance to prove that the polluter pays principle means something and apply it to those who have profited the most.

text:
Market Definition

The sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market encompasses sustainable and low-carbon aviation fuels developed, produced, blended, distributed, and utilized as alternatives to conventional fossil-based jet fuel across commercial, military, business, and unmanned aviation platforms. These fuels are designed to reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while supporting long-term aviation decarbonization, energy diversification, and regulatory sustainability targets. SAF solutions include bio-based fuels, synthetic e-fuels, and emerging hydrogen-based aviation fuels compatible with evolving aircraft propulsion technologies and airport fueling ecosystems.

Modern sustainable aviation fuel solutions are developed using multiple advanced feedstocks, conversion pathways, and fuel production technologies such as hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), Fischer-Tropsch (FT), alcohol-to-jet (ATJ), catalytic hydrothermolysis jet (CHJ), co-processing, and synthetic power-to-liquid (PtL) e-fuel systems. These fuels are produced from feedstocks including used cooking oil (UCO), agricultural residues, municipal solid waste (MSW), forestry residues, algae, ethanol-based sources, renewable electricity, and captured carbon dioxide (CO2). SAF deployment varies significantly based on fuel certification limits, blending capacities, feedstock availability, production economics, refinery infrastructure, regulatory incentives, and airline sustainability commitments.

As the aviation industry globally transitions toward net-zero emission targets and energy-resilient aviation ecosystems, sustainable aviation fuel is increasingly becoming a critical pillar of aviation decarbonization strategies. These fuels enable airlines, military operators, governments, and aviation stakeholders to reduce carbon emissions without requiring immediate replacement of existing aircraft fleets, while supporting long-term environmental compliance, fuel security, and sustainable aviation operations across both developed and emerging economies.

Consumers pay more and more attention to how companies treat the environment. Here is how GoGreen Plus helps businesses of every size in Brazil ship with fewer emissions, and how to add it to your shipments.

What is GoGreen Plus?

GoGreen Plus is a DHL Express solution that lets businesses contribute to cutting the carbon emissions of their shipments. When you join, DHL channels funds into buying and using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

SAF is a biofuel produced from renewable sources and can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by up to 80% compared with fossil fuels. Even if your shipment does not fly on an aircraft running on SAF, your participation helps fund the use of this fuel across the DHL network.

Why does GoGreen Plus matter for your business?

Consumers pay more and more attention to how companies treat the environment, and many prefer to buy from businesses that care about it. That makes sustainability a competitive advantage, whatever the size of your company.

A small e-commerce business that ships its products by air can shrink the carbon footprint of its shipments and show its commitment to sustainability to win over conscious shoppers. For a company that ships internationally all the time, GoGreen Plus also strengthens its image with investors and partners who value responsible environmental practices.

What are the benefits of GoGreen Plus?

On top of the investment in sustainable aviation fuel, businesses that choose GoGreen Plus get:

CO₂ calculation: a reliable calculation of the emissions of your shipments.

Insetting, an absolute CO₂ reduction: climate action taken inside your own value chain.

Climate neutral shipping: offsetting of CO₂ emissions through approved environmental protection programs.

End-to-end credibility: the whole process is verified by an independent body accredited by Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS).

Carbon report and certification: the GoGreen Plus Carbon Management certification, developed by SGS, supports your company's carbon management.

How does GoGreen Plus work?

DHL Express offers two ways to use GoGreen Plus.

Option 1: on a contract basis

With a DHL account and contract, your business tailors its GoGreen mix. The basic GoGreen option includes CO₂e reduction levels of up to 70%. With a tailored SAF investment contract, the reduction can reach 80% compared with fossil fuels. An independent auditor verifies the reduction values every year.

With the basic contract, your business invests in CO₂ reduction (insetting) across all its international air express shipments. Alternative reduction levels and CO₂e WTW emission reports are only available on a contract basis.

Option 2: one shipment at a time on MyDHL+

If you ship through MyDHL+, as a guest or with an account that has no GoGreen Plus in its contract, you can add GoGreen Plus to any individual shipment, with a standard CO₂e reduction of around 30%. It is a good fit for small and medium-sized businesses and e-commerce companies with smaller loads.

How do you add GoGreen Plus to a shipment?

On MyDHL+: when you create your shipment on MyDHL+, add GoGreen Plus to it.

On a contract: talk to your DHL Express sales representative or fill in the form on the DHL Express Brazil GoGreen Plus page (in Portuguese).

Shipping from a DHL store in Brazil? The team can guide you on adding GoGreen Plus to your shipment. Find your nearest DHL store.

What else is DHL doing to cut emissions?

Fuel optimization: balancing aircraft weight and choosing fuel-efficient carriers.

Fleet renewal: when buying new aircraft, DHL invests in alternative energy solutions that are fuel efficient and SAF capable.

Ground operations: electrification and hydrogen technologies to cut emissions on the ground.

Innovation: DHL supports the development of electric aircraft and SAF production plants, and has ordered up to 12 fully electric aircraft, with deliveries from 2027.

With GoGreen Plus, your business contributes to a greener future while building customer trust and loyalty. Create your shipment on MyDHL+, open a DHL Express account to get GoGreen Plus on a contract, or visit a DHL store.

On the afternoon of Monday, August 31, the "Keio University SDGs Conference—Keio University Student Conference (KUSC) 2026 Field Trip" was held at the Japan Airlines (JAL) Sky Museum at Haneda Airport. Building on the success of summer camps held on campus over the past four years, this was the first time in the conference's five-year history that it was held off-campus. On the day, approximately 40 Keio students, ranging from elementary school to university level, gathered at the JAL Sky Museum to deepen their understanding of sustainability initiatives in the aviation industry. Students from the affiliated schools and the university exchanged opinions with JAL employees.

The "Keio University Student Conference (KUSC)" is an initiative where selected university students from all faculties deepen their knowledge through lectures by experts and discuss visions, goals, and targets during the spring semester. In the fall semester, they consider actions to be implemented as Keio University's SDGs. Ultimately, the recommendations compiled through these discussions are handed to the President. Through this field trip and the specific initiatives of a single corporation, participants were able to gain a broad perspective that extends beyond SDGs within Keio.

On the day, participants first toured the museum individually before splitting into seven groups to tour the hangar while receiving explanations from JAL employees. Afterward, Vice-President Akiyō Okuda expressed gratitude to JAL and shared her expectations for the project. This was followed by a lecture from Shinnosuke Fukuda of JAL's Sustainability Promotion Department on challenges in the aviation industry and the promotion of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), which is made from sustainable raw materials such as waste cooking oil and biomass. The group discussion themes following the lecture were "The Value of Airplanes (Let's imagine a world without them)" for the first half, and "Ways to Promote SAF (Let's consider the current status of price and volume)" for the second half. Various JAL employees, including sustainability promotion staff, maintenance crew, and cabin attendants, joined the discussions with one employee per group.

In the final group presentations of the program, proposals were made such as "Ways to Promote SAF," "Holding exhibitions and stamp rallies at the Mita Festival," and "Building a system led by local governments to collect and reuse household waste oil." In the final review, Kazuya Kameyama, General Manager of JAL's Sustainability Promotion Department, indicated that the proposals from participants might be utilized in JAL's future initiatives. For the Keio students, it was a day to interact directly with adults working to promote SDGs in a corporate setting and to feel their enthusiasm firsthand.

title: Stakeholders urge EU prevent e-HEFA from counting toward e-SAF mandate
description:
The European Commission’s REFuelEU Aviation mandate requires aviation fuel suppliers to supply a minimum share of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) at European Airports.
The mandate starts at 2% of the overall aviation fuel supply in 2025, ramping up to 70% by 2050.
ReFuelEU Aviation regulations prevent SAF produced from food- and crop-based feedstocks from meeting the mandate.
The EU’s SAF mandate defines e-SAF to include power-to-liquid (PtL) fuels produced using green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide.
In the letter, the stakeholders express concern that the EU could allow electrolytic hydrogen used in traditional SAF production to be counted toward the e-SAF sub-mandate.
text:
A coalition of stakeholders on Sept. 14 sent a letter to leaders of the European Commission urging them to resist pressure to allow electrolytic hydrogen used an intermediate processing input to be counted towards the European Union’s e-SAF requirement.

The European Commission’s REFuelEU Aviation mandate requires aviation fuel suppliers to supply a minimum share of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) at European Airports. The mandate starts at 2% of the overall aviation fuel supply in 2025, ramping up to 70% by 2050. ReFuelEU Aviation regulations prevent SAF produced from food- and crop-based feedstocks from meeting the mandate. The program also includes a sub-mandate for synthetic fuels (e-SAF) that starts at 1.2% in 2030 and expands to 35% in 2050.

The EU’s SAF mandate defines e-SAF to include power-to-liquid (PtL) fuels produced using green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide.

Hydrogen is a critical input for SAF production and is sued in the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) process, as well as PtL technologies and alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) processes. Most hydrogen is currently sourced from natural gas reforming. Electrolytic hydrogen, however, is produced by using an electric current to split water molecules.

In the letter, the stakeholders express concern that the EU could allow electrolytic hydrogen used in traditional SAF production to be counted toward the e-SAF sub-mandate.

“While this accounting trick is currently primarily being pushed to bypass the ReFuelEU e-SAF targets, its approval would establish a dangerous regulatory precedent across the entire EU transport framework,” they wrote. “If this interpretation prevails, electrolytic hydrogen used in processes like HEFA/HVO hydrotreatment would generate a synthetic fuel share in resulting biofuel outputs. This would allow existing biofuel refiners to claim they are delivering e-fuels, without building new synthetic fuel plants.”

Allowing traditional SAF produced with electrolytic hydrogen to count towards the e-SAF mandate would risk development in e-SAF plants, the groups explained. “This risks rewarding inaction and allowing incumbent suppliers to capture additional profits from existing assets,” they wrote. “The fuel volumes produced via this new ‘e-HEFA’ compliance route could potentially be sold just below the price of genuine e-SAF while benefiting from substantially lower production costs, allowing suppliers to capture disproportionate economic margins without delivering genuine synthetic fuel capacity nor offering SAF volumes at significantly lower transactional prices that those of genuine e-SAF.”

Analysis completed by the European Federation for Transport and Environment indicates the “e-HEFA” workaround could displace up to 50% of the 2030-2031 e-SAF targets and up to 25% of the 2032-2034 targets.

A full copy of the letter is available on the European Federation for Transport and Environment website.

India’s jet fuel demand is projected to increase from about 192,000 barrels per day in 2024 to 277,000 barrels per day by 2031, creating a larger market for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), according to a report by S&P Global Energy and the SAF Association. The findings were released at the 2nd India SAF Conclave.

The government’s SAF blending roadmap begins with a 1 per cent mandate in 2027, rising to 2 per cent in 2028 and 5 per cent in 2030. The policy is intended to support aviation decarbonisation while encouraging the development of domestic SAF production and supply chains.

The report estimates that India’s SAF demand will reach 46,000 t in 2027 before increasing to 250,000 t in 2030. It also identifies India’s aviation sector as one of the fastest-growing sources of refined product demand through 2060, supported by rising middle-class mobility, higher domestic and international travel, airport development and airline fleet additions.

Aviation fuel consumption softened during mid-2026, with July demand falling to about 180,000 barrels per day amid weaker flight activity, higher operating costs and supply disruptions. However, consumption during the first half of 2026 still increased by nearly 2 per cent year on year, indicating that the recent weakness has not altered the longer-term growth outlook.

Passenger traffic, low-cost aviation and international connectivity are expected to remain important demand drivers. New infrastructure, including Navi Mumbai International Airport and Jewar Airport in Noida, is intended to ease capacity constraints, while international seat capacity is expanding faster than domestic capacity in 2026. Policy measures such as the UDAN regional connectivity scheme and an aviation turbine fuel (ATF) pricing stabilisation mechanism, including a fixed ATF price in Delhi and a dedicated fund, are also expected to improve cost visibility for airlines.

text:
One of Vylor’s first initiatives in Brazil after completing its spin-off from Corteva will be an unusual one: introducing Indian mustard as a feedstock for biofuel production.

The company is targeting sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, as well as hydrotreated vegetable oil, or HVO, a renewable diesel that is chemically similar to fossil diesel and can be used in heavy-duty vehicles without engine modifications.

Sign Up The AgriBiz Weekly, a newsletter for global investors

Brazilian production of these fuels, particularly SAF, has so far centered largely on soybean oil, although companies are developing alternative feedstocks including macauba (a Brazilian palm), animal fats and waste oils such as used cooking oil.

Vylor inherited the project from Corteva through Etlas, a joint venture with BP that plans to produce biofuels from mustard, canola and sunflower.

Etlas aims to produce 1 million metric tons of feedstock annually by 2030, enough to support production of 800,000 metric tons of biofuels a year. Initial supplies are expected in 2027, initially for testing in biofuel production and refinery co-processing.

“We imported some hybrids from India, following the regulatory process, to conduct the first trials,” Anelcindo Souza, Vylor’s marketing director for Brazil and Paraguay, said in an interview. “We’re learning how the crop performs in Brazil.”

Commercial contracts have not yet been signed and will be handled by Etlas, Souza said.

Competitive Advantages

Indian mustard could offer significant advantages over other agricultural feedstocks used to produce biofuels, according to Vylor.

The crop is well suited to hot, dry conditions and has a short growing cycle of about 30 to 60 days. Those characteristics could make it attractive in areas where temperature and rainfall patterns make safrinha corn, sorghum or cotton — crops planted after the main summer harvest — economically or agronomically challenging.

Vylor has identified 5 million hectares (12.4 million acres) in northern Brazil with potential for Indian mustard as a second crop. Of that area, between 700,000 and 1 million hectares (1.7 million to 2.5 million acres) currently remain fallow during that planting window.

“Farmers aren’t planting during that window because neither corn nor sorghum makes financial sense,” Souza said.

Indian mustard seeds have an oil yield of about 35% to 40% after crushing, Souza said. That compares with roughly 20% for soybeans and about 30% for macauba, another emerging feedstock being considered for SAF.

The initiative remains at an early stage, but Etlas expects its first commercial-scale planting in 2028, said William Weber, Vylor’s president for its Brazil and Paraguay commercial unit. The venture has not disclosed a target acreage.

“We tested it for three years, and now we’re designing the supply chain so it can fit into the second-crop window in regions facing climate constraints,” Weber said. Despite the seed’s small size, he added, its oil potential is significant.

Hybrid Wheat

Vylor announced Thursday that it had completed its separation from Corteva, becoming an independent, publicly traded company. Its shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker VYLR.

The company starts out with a technology portfolio valued at $19 billion and plans 12 technology-platform launches through 2035 targeting some of Brazil’s largest crops, including soybeans, corn and wheat.

Among them is Xpedite, Vylor’s proprietary system for developing hybrid wheat. Company research indicates the technology can deliver consistently high productivity and greater yield stability, including improved resilience to disease and drought.

Corteva’s predecessor businesses helped pioneer commercial hybrid corn seeds nearly a century ago, and Vylor is now seeking to bring a similar technological shift to wheat.

Vylor also plans seven corn-related launches over the next decade. One technology under testing has shown yield gains of as much as 3.3 bags per hectare, or about 198 kilograms per hectare, compared with seed technologies currently prevalent in the market — a bag weighs 60 kilograms.

The company’s corn pipeline also includes a gene-editing platform aimed at improving disease resistance.

For soybeans, Vylor plans four launches through 2035, including a proprietary platform that the company says would provide the broadest spectrum of insect control on the market.

The products stem from research and development spending that, according to Vylor, historically amounted to about 10% of annual sales from the seed and genetics businesses that now make up the independent company.

text:
As the cost of fuel rises, a coalition of aviation companies and agricultural groups are partnering to produce a sustainable jet fuel in Georgia.

The Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition includes Delta Air Lines, the Metro Atlanta Chamber, the Georgia Forestry Association, and the Georgia Farm Bureau. The group will research, develop, and produce a new biofuel using timber waste, and farming materials.

Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper said this will be a boost for industries that are still recovering from Hurricane Helene.

“We're building markets for producers, for timberland owners and meeting a demand for businesses like Delta that ensures that they're addressing concerns of their customers and others. So it is a win-win for us and it couldn't come at a better time.”

Over the next year the SAF Coalition will be working towards having a product demonstration. Metro Atlanta Cahmber CEO Katie Kirkpatrick said she thinks that’s achievable.

“Our first steps will be to create functional groups that will zero in on research, policy, feedstock and supply chain, partner outreach, and perhaps more,” Kirkpatrick said. “We will identify supply and demand, identify the obstacles and barriers, hire a dedicated GRA scholar, which will be at Georgia Southern.”

A panel of SAF partners also identified challenges that the group will navigate. Charlotte Lollar is the director of SAF and Emissions at Delta. She said the demand is there, but the challenge will be making enough biofuel at the right price to meet it.

“So availability is definitely a challenge, and with nascency comes costs,” Lollar said. “Right now it is very, very expensive. And that's why having underpinning policy support to help ramp up and scale and ultimately reduce those costs is critical.”

State Legislators recently passed House Bill 134, known as Keep Georgia Forested Act. The bill created new income tax credits for forestry manufacturing facilities to support renewable fuels.

Delta Air Lines President Peter Carter said the coalition has all the right partners to be successful.

Delta Air Lines is aiming to use 100% sustainable fuel by 2050. The SAF coalition is estimating locally made sustainable fuel will be at Hartfield-Jackson airport within 5 years.

title: Aether Fuels Produces ASTM-Compliant Synthetic Aviation Fuel in Integrated Demonstration
description:
Aether Fuels has successfully operated a fully integrated demonstration line producing synthetic aviation fuel that meets ASTM D7566 specifications, marking a step toward commercial deployment of its Aurora sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) technology.
The system converted renewable natural gas derived from Kentucky landfill gas and captured industrial carbon dioxide into fully upgraded synthetic aviation fuel.
"This demonstration proves Aether's ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel," said Dhaval Shah, chief technology officer of Aether Fuels.
Aether projects that fuel from these facilities could achieve lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions reductions exceeding 70% compared with conventional fossil jet fuel.
Aether CEO and co-founder Conor Madigan said the integrated demonstration follows the company's earlier work validating individual components of the Aurora platform and scaling up its technology in standalone demonstration units.
text:
Aether Fuels has successfully operated a fully integrated demonstration line producing synthetic aviation fuel that meets ASTM D7566 specifications, marking a step toward commercial deployment of its Aurora sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) technology.

The demonstration, conducted at RTI International in North Carolina, combined Aether's 2.5-barrel-per-day Aurora Tri-Converter and Upgrader units with RTI's existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor. The system converted renewable natural gas derived from Kentucky landfill gas and captured industrial carbon dioxide into fully upgraded synthetic aviation fuel.

Independent testing by AmSpec confirmed that fuel samples met the applicable ASTM D7566 specifications for Fischer-Tropsch Synthesized Paraffinic Kerosene (FT-SPK). Under the standard, qualifying FT-SPK can be blended with conventional jet fuel at concentrations of up to 50% without modifications to existing aircraft or airport fueling infrastructure.

"This demonstration proves Aether's ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel," said Dhaval Shah, chief technology officer of Aether Fuels.

The demonstration builds on previous testing of Aether's standalone Tri-Converter technology and provides engineering data for the company's planned Project Beacon facility in Singapore.

Project Beacon is designed to produce approximately 2,000 metric tons of SAF annually, equivalent to 50 barrels per day. Aether said the latest demonstration will inform the facility's design and help reduce technical risks ahead of commercial deployment.

The company is also developing additional commercial projects intended to produce ASTM-compliant SAF. Aether projects that fuel from these facilities could achieve lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions reductions exceeding 70% compared with conventional fossil jet fuel.

Aether CEO and co-founder Conor Madigan said the integrated demonstration follows the company's earlier work validating individual components of the Aurora platform and scaling up its technology in standalone demonstration units.

title: Implications of Potential US Diesel Export Ban and Pressure on Europe - ResourceWise
description:
A potential US diesel export ban is becoming more than a domestic fuel-price debate.
Washington could use a potential diesel export ban to pressure France and Germany into releasing emergency stocks.
Lower diesel prices could squeeze soybean oil-based biofuel margins and prompt adjustments in D4 RIN prices.
Why Is a US Diesel Export Ban Being Discussed?
US diesel exports in June were 12% higher than in January, while jet fuel exports rose approximately 25% over the same period.
text:
A potential US diesel export ban is becoming more than a domestic fuel-price debate. It could also become a bargaining chip to pressure Europe into releasing emergency supplies.

Reuters reported that the Trump administration has told France and Germany to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help ease global fuel prices or face a possible US export ban.

The immediate appeal is straightforward: keep more American diesel at home or persuade European governments to put additional barrels into circulation. Either approach could offer relief in a tight market.

But a recent Prima CarbonZero analyst report highlights why restricting exports could produce consequences that extend well beyond diesel. An initial price decline could weaken refinery economics, reduce production of other fuels, and change the balance between fossil diesel, renewable fuels, and compliance credits.

Key Takeaways

The export threat could provide leverage. Washington could use a potential diesel export ban to pressure France and Germany into releasing emergency stocks.

Domestic price relief could be temporary. As storage fills and margins weaken, refiners could cut output, tightening gasoline and jet fuel supplies.

Biofuel economics could shift. Lower diesel prices could squeeze soybean oil-based biofuel margins and prompt adjustments in D4 RIN prices.

Policy details will shape the impact. European stock releases, the potential ban’s scope and duration, and refinery responses will determine whether intervention eases pressure or creates new constraints.

Why Is a US Diesel Export Ban Being Discussed?

Strong domestic demand, high exports, and low inventories have put diesel prices under pressure. This holds true even as refiners run hard to capture attractive margins.

According to a Prima CarbonZero analysis, reduced global middle distillate supply associated with conflict in the Middle East has increased demand for US exports. US diesel exports in June were 12% higher than in January, while jet fuel exports rose approximately 25% over the same period.

Those international supply pressures are colliding with domestic concerns about fuel affordability, particularly among farmers.

Could the Threat Encourage France and Germany to Release Stocks?

The potential leverage comes from the consequences of losing access to US diesel exports. In an already constrained international market, removing those barrels could intensify competition for replacement supplies.

Releasing emergency diesel stocks could help ease that pressure while giving Washington an alternative to restricting exports. In this scenario, the threat functions as a negotiating tool intended to bring additional supply into the market.

However, a stock release and an export ban work differently. A release makes stored fuel available for consumption. A ban initially redirects existing US production toward the domestic market, with the eventual outcome depending on storage capacity and refiners’ willingness to maintain output.

Emergency stocks also provide a temporary buffer. They cannot indefinitely compensate for disrupted supply or insufficient production.

The central concern comes down to whether diplomatic pressure can secure meaningful near-term relief and whether that relief can bridge the market to more sustainable supply conditions.

Why Might Domestic Price Relief Be Short-Lived?

Keeping export barrels in the United States could initially increase domestic availability and push diesel prices lower. But the Prima CarbonZero report identifies a limit to that benefit: spare storage capacity.

Once refiners lose access to overseas buyers, surplus diesel must find a domestic customer or be stored. As storage fills and diesel margins weaken, refiners could reduce processing rates.

That response would affect more than diesel. Refineries produce multiple fuels, so lower utilization could also reduce gasoline and jet fuel supply.

The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers warns that restricting diesel exports could consequently raise prices for those products. The group also points to the approaching home heating oil season as a particularly difficult time to constrain refinery output.

Lifting a temporary ban could create another adjustment. Domestic diesel prices would reconnect with a potentially tighter international market, exposing buyers to a renewed price increase.

A policy intended to provide immediate relief could therefore exchange today's price pressure for production cuts and volatility later.

What Would This Mean for Renewable Diesel and Biodiesel?

The implications would extend into biofuel margins and compliance markets.

The relationship between soybean oil and heating oil prices is a key transmission channel. If a ban pushed domestic diesel and heating oil prices lower while soybean oil remained relatively expensive, the feedstock-to-fuel balance could become less favorable for soybean oil-based biofuel production.

The Prima CarbonZero analyst report suggests that D4 Renewable Identification Number prices would need to respond to help rebalance biofuel economics. The size and timing of that adjustment would depend on the broader market response.

For biofuel participants, the relevant signal is therefore the interaction among fuel prices, feedstock costs, refinery output, and compliance credits.

What Should Fuel Market Participants Watch?

The most consequential outcome may be whether the export threat prompts European stock releases without becoming an enacted restriction.

If a ban does proceed, its scope and duration will matter alongside storage availability, refinery utilization, and movements in fuel and credit prices.

A measure aimed at lowering the price of one fuel can reshape production and the economy across several connected markets. Understanding those relationships will be essential to assessing whether any intervention offers lasting relief or simply moves the pressure elsewhere.

Put Policy Headlines Into a Broader Biofuels Market Context

The diesel export debate illustrates how policy decisions can ripple through fuel prices, feedstock demand, and biofuel margins. Understanding those connections is essential to assessing your next commercial move.

Get expert context to help evaluate supply risks, pricing pressures, and emerging opportunities.

TOP STORY

FEATURE: Canada’s new nature taskforce begins shaping foundation of country’s nature market

Canada’s nature finance taskforce will look to set the foundation for how conservation and ecosystem markets advance in the country, starting with defining who should be involved and how they can contribute.

AMERICAS

ANALYSIS: Nature-related shareholder resolutions defy regulatory upheaval as focus shifts to regen agriculture in 2026

Nature-related shareholder resolutions persisted through US regulatory upheaval in the 2026 proxy season, as investor attention shifted towards regenerative agriculture, according to Carbon Pulse analysis.

A coalition of legal experts and environmental groups from across Latin America launched a template of a law in Mexico City on Thursday to support legislators in criminalising the most severe forms of environmental harm and destruction.

A proposed road between Brazil and Peru in the Amazon could result in up to 133,800 hectares of additional deforestation over 20 years and put Acre’s jurisdictional REDD+ (J-REDD+) goals at risk, according to a report published on Wednesday.

China’s Shenzhen and Hong Kong should move from individual nature-based solutions (NbS) projects towards a landscape-scale portfolio in the Shenzhen River-Deep Bay basin, with the approach eventually expanded across the Greater Bay Area (GBA), a new report said.

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is preparing a $200,000 project to help mobilise private investment in biodiversity conservation through nature credits in Mongolia.

An alliance of carbon project developers and conservation groups have called on the Australian government to maintain and update guidance on carbon credit use once the Climate Active scheme wraps up, to ensure future demand.

Farming peak body wants more ACCUs produced from farms, less from forests

Australia’s agricultural peak body has pushed for greater use of carbon credits that are generated at farms themselves, while at the same time calling for guardrails against carbon sequestration projects that have the potential to disrupt food and fibre production.

A European intergovernmental organisation has set aside €600,000 to fund initiatives that strengthen forest biodiversity conservation, including by deepening understanding of nature credits.

BITE-SIZED UPDATES FROM AROUND THE WORLD

EMEA

EU nature credits – The European Commission’s expert group on nature credits is holding its fourth meeting over Oct.1-2. The gathering aims to advance the EU’s ongoing work to design the overarching frameworks for a bloc-wide nature credit market by the end of next year. The meeting comes as the European Commission is set to present its plans at the COP17 UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, next month.

ASIA PACIFIC

World Congress on Snakes – The Sri Lankan city of Kandy is hosting the first World Congress on Snakes from Oct. 1-4 covering conservation, snake biology, and public health. More than 400 delegates from 25 countries are expected to attend the conference, reported Mongabay. The event will be held under 12 themes ranging from snake biology to policies for human coexistence with snakes. These include safeguarding snakes and their habitats under global pressure, and the management of captive snakes for conservation.

Target doubled – The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) will aim to double its annual financing to $20 bln by 2030, prioritising infrastructure for climate resilience, renewable energy, and nature conservation, alongside other focus areas like digital transformation and regional connectivity. This was announced by AIIB President Jiayi Zou at the development bank’s 11th annual meeting in Qatar this week, marking the start of its second decade of operation. AIIB has said that it is devoting more attention to integrating biodiversity and nature-based solutions into its infrastructure investment considerations.

Biochar potential – Japanese developer Asian Gateway’s proposal to launch a feasibility study for rice husk-based biochar production in Cambodia’s Battambang province has been selected for government grants. The study aims to verify the commercial viability of an entire value chain, from converting rice husks into biochar and applying it to farmland to conducting MRV and generating credits under the Joint Crediting Mechanism. It will also consider an integrated approach that applies both the alternate wetting and drying method and rice-husk derived biochar to the same fields.

AMERICAS

Deep sea – Conservation groups filed a lawsuit on Wednesday challenging the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s certification of a seabed mineral exploration application. The lawsuit, from Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi and the Center for Biological Diversity, represented by Earthjustice, alleged that the authority had breached requirements on transparency and public participation. The application from the Metals Company USA was the first to receive certification for deep-sea mining exploration since President Trump took office, while several other applications are pending, according to the centre.

Another US mining dispute – The Centre for Biological Diversity and Patagonia Area Resource Alliance have sued the Trump administration in the US District Court for the District of Arizona over its decision to approve the expansion of South32’s Hermosa mine onto federal public lands in southern Arizona. The lawsuit challenges approvals by the US Forest Service and US Fish and Wildlife Service that would expand industrial mining across more than 21,000 hectares of public land in the Coronado National Forest. The mine is located in the Patagonia Mountains of Arizona, one of the state’s most biodiverse and ecologically significant mountain ranges.

Species recovery – Two US senators have presented draft legislation to change the implementation of the US Endangered Species Act’s species recovery efforts. The proposals aim to standardise conservation efforts, encourage conservation efforts by private landowners, and help endangered species to recover, said senators Adam Schiff and Pete Ricketts. The bipartisan bill comes amid a wider debate over the future of the Endangered Species Act, including lawsuits by 21 states challenging recent Trump administration changes to existing species protections.

Georgia SAF coalition – A group of Georgia businesses, forestry, and agriculture producers have teamed up to create the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new partnership focused on positioning the state as a US leader in sustainable aviation fuel research and production. The coalition aims to accelerate the growth of agri- and forestry-derived SAF by coordinating public-private partnerships, better aligning university research with industry needs, and considering new avenues to attract investment. The coalition is aiming to build upon momentum created by the Keep Georgia Forested Act, legislation that encourages investment into forestry manufacturing, including the production of biofuels from Georgia-based feedstocks.

Wetland restoration – Energy company Orsted announced this week it has started construction of its Blackwater Solar project in New Mexico, alongside a $100,000 investment in local wetland conservation. The funding will support restoration of a site near Melrose, through a partnership with Playa Lakes Joint Venture. The initiative will focus on restoring bird habitat and improving the biological function of the wetland.

INTERNATIONAL

Current affairs – Marine technology company Blue Carbon International (BCI) and environmental finance advisory AeonLoop announced a partnership via LinkedIn this week to help governments measure the value of marine ecosystems and develop financial structures to attract institutional investment. The companies said they would combine BCI’s marine science and natural-capital accounting capabilities with AeonLoop’s expertise in financial structuring, Article 6 programme design, and access to capital markets. The partnership targets new sovereign opportunities beyond BCI’s existing work in the Bahamas, with the companies potentially jointly marketing their services and involving one another in new engagements.
