text:
Two Louisville men were arrested early Tuesday at an Evansville Rally's on a preliminary organized-theft charge after a grease hauler's driver blocked in their van.

Police say the van held about 300 gallons of used cooking oil, significantly more than was taken from Rally's. The affidavit names no other victims.

EVANSVILLE — When police pulled into the Rally's on East Morgan Avenue early Tuesday, a semi-truck had a white Ford Transit van boxed in at the north end of the lot. Yellow lights flashed atop the van, the kind commonly affixed to utility vehicles.

The work van was backed up to the Rally's used cooking oil container, and two men in yellow reflective vests stood near its front.

The semi's driver worked for Mahoney Environmental, the multinational company that collects Rally's and many other restaurants spent fryer oil, he said. He told officers he had driven by, spotted the van near the oil tank and suspected theft — a form of thievery that has grown increasingly common in this line of work. He called 911 and trapped the van with his truck, according to police reports reviewed by the Courier & Press.

Officers arrested the men in the yellow vests — Jonatan Pozo Wilson, 29, and Roelmis Pozo Turcaz, 53, who told officers they were from Louisville — on a preliminary charge of organized theft, a Level 6 felony. Both were held without bond Wednesday in the Vanderburgh County jail pending a first court appearance. Their initial hearings were scheduled for later that day.

The oil taken from Rally's was worth just $588, its general manager and the Mahoney driver told police. But the scene fit a pattern unfolding behind restaurants nationwide.

Used cooking oil, once the object of an undesirable disposal chore, has become a prized ingredient in renewable diesel and other biofuels — and a lucrative target for thieves.

The North American Renderers Association, an industry trade group, estimates that $300 million to $500 million worth is stolen each year, a figure it calls conservative.

Police suspect Rally's was not the Wilson's and Turcaz's only stop. An inventory search before the van was towed allegedly turned up two large containers: one empty, the other holding roughly 300 gallons of oil. That was "significantly greater" than the amount taken from Rally's, "indicating there were additional sources the oil had been taken from," officer Joshua Myers wrote in sworn affidavits supporting the men's arrests.

The affidavits do not say how much oil came from Rally's or where the rest originated. EPD spokesman Sgt. Anthony Aussieker said the department had nothing to add to the report and that "there are no additional reports" of such oil thefts in Evansville.

When asked, neither Wilson nor Turcaz could name the company they worked for, according to the affidavits. They showed officers a supposed waste oil collection agreement for a Louisville business, Latin Food & Bakery. Police noted it contained numerous typos. Both said they worked for a man named Mario, but Turcaz told Patrolman Herbert Adams, who read the men their rights in Spanish, that he did not know Mario's last name.

A lucrative black market

A Rally's shift manager told Evansville police she had never seen the men, and the general manager said only Mahoney Environmental is contracted to collect the restaurant's oil. But both said they had heard of unauthorized collectors taking oil from other area businesses.

Restaurants typically pour spent fryer oil into outdoor bins, contracted collectors pump it out and sell it to fuel producers and a few other business sectors. Mahoney has been owned since 2020 by Neste, which calls itself the world's leading producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel.

The Evansville arrests were at least the second of their kind in Indiana this month.

On Sept. 17, the owner of King Gyros in Plymouth called 911 at 2:46 a.m. to report he had video of a truck taking his restaurant's oil. The truck returned at 3:37 a.m., and police arrived while two men were still on the property. Eliodanys C. Plutin, 26, of Indianapolis, and Omar P. Cutino, 38, of Louisville, were arrested on theft and organized theft charges, Plymouth radio station WTCA reported. Mahoney collects King Gyros' oil, too.

In Kentucky in October 2025, Bowling Green police arrested two Louisville men after an employee of Darling Ingredients, another oil collector, reported seeing them take oil from containers behind several restaurants, WBKO-TV reported. One told officers the pair were "trying to start a company from 'picking oil.'" And in Louisville this year, according to Mahoney, a worker at a bowling alley spotted an old ambulance backing up to one of the company's containers. The ambulance and the oil were seized.

The vests, lights and paperwork in Evansville echo tactics that an investigator for a grease recycler described to St. Louis Magazine this year.

Thieves often wear reflective vests and hard hats to appear like regular workers and can drain a restaurant's bin in as little as five minutes. If police happen upon them, they'll often claim the restaurant's regular hauler subcontracted them, the investigator said.

Some thefts have drawn federal racketeering charges. In Iowa, 19 people were charged in a scheme prosecutors say involved stealing oil from restaurants in 10 states, including Indiana and Kentucky, and laundering the proceeds. Two pleaded guilty to racketeering conspiracy this month; the rest are set for trial in April. In Missouri, prosecutors accuse the owner of a septic company of buying stolen grease, forging paperwork to disguise its origin and selling it to a Minnesota company that paid him about $1.3 million.

Regulatory changes could fuel future thefts

The grease is valuable in large part due to fuel regulations.

The federal Renewable Fuel Standard requires fuel companies to blend in renewable fuel, and producers who make it from used cooking oil generate credits they can sell to companies that fall short. California subsidizes diesel made from recycled fats; used cooking oil is the basis for 15% to 20% of the state's diesel market, the agriculture publication Ambrook reported in January.

And federal regulatory changes made under the Trump administration, largely aimed at limiting certain Chinese imports, could have the indirect of effect of making the oil an even more valuable target for thieves and organized crime networks.

A federal clean fuel tax credit, reworked in the tax-and-spending law President Donald Trump signed last year, now requires feedstocks from the U.S., Canada or Mexico — a change designed to block large imports of used cooking oil from nations outside of North America, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation.

"With the restriction on imports, that means all domestic sources and feedstocks are going to become more valuable," Montana State University agricultural economist Andrew Swanson told Ambrook.

Sumit Majumdar, CEO of Buffalo Biodiesel, a used cooking oil recycler, put it this way: "There's a lot of people making a lot of money ... It's the legitimate operators that are getting pushed out."

title: France Backs Double-Auction Mechanism To Accelerate Synthetic Aviation Fuel Development
description:
Among the options identified to accelerate the development of these fuels, the government backs the principle of a mechanism known as "double auction".
Through the scheme being prepared, France will join Germany, Luxembourg and Austria among the coalition members that have proposed a double-auction mechanism for these fuels.
The use of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) is one of the main levers for decarbonizing the sector, in line with the industry's national roadmap.
Sustainable aviation fuels, including synthetic ones referred to as eCAD, are subject to specific incorporation obligations under the European ReFuelEU Aviation regulation, obligations set to intensify in the coming years.
The state is already supporting initial sustainable aviation fuel production projects, notably through the CarbAero call for projects, funded with 100 million euros and backing four projects.
text:
The report on synthetic aviation fuels, commissioned in June 2025 to the general inspectorate of finance (IGF) and the general inspectorate of environment and sustainable development (IGEDD), was delivered on Wednesday September 23 to Philippe Tabarot, Minister of Transport, and to Maud Brégeon, Minister in charge of Energy. Among the options identified to accelerate the development of these fuels, the government backs the principle of a mechanism known as "double auction".

A European coalition of early movers

France is among the member states engaged in the coalition of pioneers for synthetic aviation fuels, named the "e-SAF early movers coalition", launched on the initiative of the European Commission at the end of 2025. Through the scheme being prepared, France will join Germany, Luxembourg and Austria among the coalition members that have proposed a double-auction mechanism for these fuels.

Air transport accounts for 2.5% of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, according to the government statement. The use of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) is one of the main levers for decarbonizing the sector, in line with the industry's national roadmap. Sustainable aviation fuels, including synthetic ones referred to as eCAD, are subject to specific incorporation obligations under the European ReFuelEU Aviation regulation, obligations set to intensify in the coming years.

Industrial strengths to secure

It is in this context that the government mandated the IGF and IGEDD in June 2025 to carry out an evaluation mission on the development of synthetic fuels, particularly for the aviation sector. The mission aimed to detail the economic and legal obstacles to the emergence of a production industry, to assess France's industrial strengths against international competition, and to propose public policy tools.

According to the inspectorates, France has significant assets to host industrial eCAD production projects, including a competitive, low-carbon electricity mix, an advanced research and development ecosystem, and project developers already engaged. The mission also stressed the importance of maintaining the momentum of the ReFuelEU Aviation regulation to secure future investments.

A double-auction mechanism to secure investment

The proposed scheme would involve a public market intermediary tasked with signing long-term purchase contracts with eCAD producers, then reselling the volumes acquired through shorter-term contracts to aviation fuel suppliers. This mechanism would aim to provide long-term visibility to project developers, a condition deemed necessary to enable final investment decisions on production sites in France.

The state is already supporting initial sustainable aviation fuel production projects, notably through the CarbAero call for projects, funded with 100 million euros and backing four projects. The government states it intends to draw on the mission's proposals in the coming weeks to design a new public support scheme, while seeking to preserve the competitiveness of French air transport in a context described as particularly difficult for airlines, and to involve all stakeholders, including airlines, industrial players and energy companies.

text:
The country is also accelerating work on a roadmap to gradually introduce SAF into its aviation market.

The authority is surveying available feedstocks including agricultural biomass, used cooking oil and waste, as well as suitable conversion technologies.

In a recent report to the Ministry of Construction, the CAAV said its findings will be used to propose a SAF supply chain model, management measures and a phased roadmap for deployment in Vietnam.

The proposed SAF roadmap will take into account Vietnam's international commitments, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and the country's ability to develop a domestic SAF supply, while avoiding shocks to domestic airlines and the air transport market.

Vietnam has already gained initial experience in importing, supplying and using SAF, while some energy companies are also examining opportunities to produce SAF domestically.

Petrolimex Aviation imported and supplied SAF for Vietjet flights at Tan Son Nhat International Airport in 2024 and participated in SAF blending in 2025.

Vietnam Airlines used 2,200 tonnes of SAF in 2025, reducing lifecycle carbon emissions by about 5,600 tonnes, the carrier said. In May 2024, it operated a commercial passenger flight from Singapore to Hanoi using SAF, becoming the first Vietnamese airline to use the fuel on a commercial passenger flight.

On August 15, Vietjet used SAF produced by Petrolimex Aviation on its flights. Petrolimex Aviation blended and supplied 1,200cu.m of SAF for Vietjet flights.

PetroVietnam has assigned its subsidiaries, Bình Sơn Refining and Petrochemical JSC (BSR) and PetroVietnam Oil Corporation (PVOIL), to work on SAF production.

BSR has studied producing SAF using the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids technology, while PVOIL and the Vietnam Petroleum Institute have studied used cooking oil and other potential feedstocks.

To sustain long-term growth, airlines belonging to the International Air Transport Association have set a goal of achieving net zero emissions by 2050, with SAF expected to account for up to 65 per cent of the emissions reductions needed to meet that target.

However, the CAAV said airlines' readiness remained uneven, with some carriers lacking specific SAF plans or sufficient information to assess their ability to deploy the fuel. In addition, existing activities had yet to form a complete SAF supply chain, and there was not enough information to fully assess the feasibility of deploying SAF nationwide.

Airport fuel infrastructure is an important part of the SAF supply chain, according to the CAAV.

At Noi Bài International Airport in Hanoi, the local aviation fuel service company has initially assessed that existing infrastructure could potentially be used for SAF or Jet A-1 blended with SAF.

Still, further assessments are needed to determine the compatibility of storage tanks, pipelines, equipment and refuelling systems, while requirements for fuel quality, testing, certification and traceability also need to be clarified.

The CAAV said it would continue working with Petrovietnam and Petrolimex on SAF production and deployment in Vietnam.

At a September 2025 meeting of the provisional Joint Committee for the ASEAN-EU Comprehensive Air Transport Agreement in Bangkok, ASEAN countries asked the EU to consider allowing SAF to be certified under both the EU's RefuelEU Aviation framework and ICAO's CORSIA standards.

Vietnam would continue to participate in discussions aimed at harmonising SAF recognition between EU and ICAO mechanisms in order to facilitate implementation by domestic carriers, the CAAV said.

CAAV Director Uong Viet Dung said that the launch of SAF would be strategically important for the long term, because it would lay the groundwork for a sustainable domestic SAF supply chain which meets international market requirements and encourages cooperation among airlines, fuel suppliers, regulators and financial institutions.

SAF is produced from renewable and sustainably sourced materials such as used cooking oil, agricultural residues, woody biomass and municipal waste. It can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared with conventional jet fuel./.VNA

text:
A new final assembly line in Saxony marks the turboprop’s shift to industrialisation, as German manufacturer Deutsche Aircraft positions itself as a test of the region’s aerospace ambitions.

Deutsche Aircraft officially inaugurated its final assembly line (FAL) at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Tuesday 29 September. The €100 million facility marks the D328eco programme’s transition from development to serial production.

The plant was completed just over three years after the ground-breaking ceremony in May 2023. It covers 60,500 sq.m. (that’s roughly eight football pitches) and is designed to build up to 48 aircraft a year. Around 250 direct jobs are expected as production of the next-generation aircraft ramps up.

“Airplanes are coming home”

Götz Ahmelmann, CEO, of airport operator Mitteldeutsche Flughafen AG, said he had used the words “airplanes are coming home” at the groundbreaking ceremony.

“Today they have arrived,” he added. “At Leipzig/ Halle Airport, aircraft will no longer only take off and land. In the future, they will also be built here and delivered from here to customers around the world. An aircraft is being built here that creates connections, in a region that understands that connectivity is a shared responsibility.”

Deutsche Aircraft’s German aircraft programme

For Deutsche Aircraft CEO Nico Neumann, the significance goes beyond the factory. It marks the return of aircraft manufacturing to Saxony and is a major milestone for the D328eco programme,” he said.

The Leipzig site complements the manufacturer’s Oberpfaffenhofen base in Bavaria. Together they create an end-to-end capability to develop, certify, industrialise, build and support a complete aircraft in Germany, which has not happened under a single German programme for more than 60 years.

Neumann described it as one of Germany’s most significant aerospace investments in recent years. “It carries forward Dornier’s pioneering legacy,” he said, calling on greater government support for aerospace ambitions.

“The FAL strengthens Germany’s resilience, competitiveness and sovereign aerospace capabilities while advancing a new generation of sustainable regional aviation.”

Marie-Christine von Hahn, principal managing director of the German Aerospace Industries Association (BDLI), backed that view. “Germany can now develop and build a complete aircraft,” she said. “Bavaria and Saxony have brought together their strengths to make this possible.”

The FAL’s September opening came nearly four months after the targeted May date given by the company’s CCO, Anastasija Visnakova. Speaking with Aerospace Global News earlier this year, she also said that Deutsche Aircraft anticipated first test flights before the end of 2026 and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certification by the end of 2027. First customer deliveries are planned for early 2028.

Flight testing under way

Flight testing began on 5 August, and the aircraft has logged more than 15 hours. Earlier this month, the company completed low-speed and high-speed taxi testing of the landing gear.

Landing gear has historically been a pain point for regional aviation programmes because of reliance on third-party suppliers and parts shortages. Deutsche Aircraft has overcome this by switching to a new supplier and securing full intellectual property rights to the system.

Existing D328 operators worldwide also stand to benefit from this testing thanks to a common architecture, better lifecycle support and improved parts availability.

The next phase for the D328eco programme

Targeting the regional air transport market, the D328eco has a range of approximately 650nm. It covers more than 90% of typical regional routes. The 40-seat aircraft delivers a spacious cabin with a 2-1 configuration, giving every passenger aisle or window access.

The D328eco offers fuel efficiency up to 50% better than comparable aircraft, according to Deutsche Aircraft. It will also be fully compatible with 100% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from day one.

With the industrial foundation for serial production of the D328eco now in place, pressure is on the German manufacturer to deliver flight-readiness activities, certification, and the first customer deliveries.

text:
Essar Future Energy (EFE) participated at the India SAF Conclave and Awards 2026, organised by SAFA in New Delhi. Centred on the theme “Powering the SAF Transition,” the conclave brought together policymakers, industry leaders and heads of organisations from across the aviation and fuels value chain to discuss how India can build and scale a sustainable aviation fuel ecosystem. Essar was also one of the sponsors at the event and representing Essar Future Energy was Vibhav Agarwal, CEO, who spoke in the session on “Scaling India’s SAF Ambition: From Feedstocks and Production to Supply Chains and Demand.”

Vibhav opened by arguing that SAF will scale only when it becomes financeable. Every commercial activity, he said, is about how risks are distributed and how stakeholders see their own benefits. For a capital-intensive industry like SAF, he argued, someone ultimately has to write the cheque, and no one will do so without a fair assessment of risk. Viewing SAF through the lens of a lender answers most questions: is enough feedstock available and can it be tied into long-term contracts; is blending certain; will airlines and blenders commit to long-term offtake; and is there open access and adequate infrastructure at airports. Reframing the problem around how lenders think, he said, is what will make SAF scalable, sustainable and a sound business model.

He stressed that businesses should stay agnostic to the production pathway, whether HEFA, ethanol-to-jet or power-to-liquid. Some are available in the short term while others will be needed as technology and commercial scale mature, so all pathways deserve attention, with local context determining how SAF progresses.

On feedstock, Vibhav disagreed with the view that India suits only certain feedstocks. With 30 to 35 million tonnes of edible oil consumed annually, ignoring used cooking oil (UCO) would be a mistake. Even a 10% collection of discards could meet domestic needs and serve global demand, as China has shown. One state’s recent efforts have already lifted collection significantly, and government is now working on standard operating procedures.

Identifying policy as the biggest gap in India’s SAF ecosystem, followed by stakeholder acceptance, he called for three things from government. First, long-term regulatory certainty, with mandates spanning 10 to 15 years rather than 2 to 3, so that projects are investable and financeable. Second, access to capital, by including SAF and biofuel projects in the harmonised master list of infrastructure projects, since lenders look for precedent that does not yet exist in India. Third, a level playing field, as the Biofuel Policy 2018 does not contemplate private SAF producers selling or distributing their product. He called for market freedom to sell and price SAF, with regulators safeguarding participants, since otherwise the product will travel out of India.

The message from Vibhav was clear: That SAF in India will scale not on ambition alone- but on whether policy certainty, access to capital and market freedom make projects investable, positioning India as a global hub serving both domestic and international demand.

text:
Petrobras has developed two research-stage blockchain applications with the Cardano Foundation and PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs to track environmental claims for sustainable aviation fuel and lifecycle data for its Diesel R renewable diesel, according to Crypto.news. The Cardano Foundation announced both projects on September 30, 2026, describing work produced through its ongoing research collaboration with Brazil’s state-controlled energy company.

Petrobras and the Cardano Foundation have built two research-stage blockchain applications: one tokenizes environmental benefits tied to sustainable aviation fuel (CS-SAF tokens), and the other records production, transport and use data for Diesel R renewable diesel. Neither project has a disclosed commercial launch date.

Key facts

The Cardano Foundation announced the projects on Sep. 30, 2026, developed with Petrobras and PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs.

The aviation application uses a Book-and-Claim model so an airline can receive a SAF environmental benefit even when another operator uses the physical fuel.

Certificates are checked against CORSIA and other recognized standards before becoming standardized tokens carrying environmental attributes, per the accompanying SAF case study.

The Foundation identifies CS-SAF as the digital token representing the aviation fuel’s environmental benefit, usable by airlines or individual journeys.

Both initiatives remain research projects, with no commercial launch date disclosed.

According to Cointelegraph, the collaboration began in 2023 with blockchain education for Petrobras employees and expanded in 2025 to energy-sector research with Ledger Labs. Cointelegraph also reported that the Cardano Foundation did not disclose fuel volumes covered by the applications — a detail Crypto.news’s report does not address either.

How the aviation token makes a claim traceable

Under the Book-and-Claim model, the environmental benefit of sustainable aviation fuel is separated from the physical fuel itself. The Foundation says that for each allocation, Cardano records the benefit’s origin and recipient, letting participants trace a claim back to the fuel certificate behind it. The proposed system addresses the risk of assigning the same environmental benefit to more than one buyer.

In the accompanying SAF case study, the certificate-checking process takes place before digital records enter the system. Certificates are checked against the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, known as CORSIA, and other recognized standards. Once verified, the case study says, the certificates become standardized tokens carrying information about their environmental attributes. Participants can issue, transfer, and inspect the tokens before retiring them when the associated benefit is claimed — a step the Foundation describes as preventing a token from being used again.

For passengers, the announcement describes an application that accepts departure and destination airports and calculates a corresponding SAF allocation. A traveler then receives a certificate showing the route, distance, and allocation, with a connection to the original fuel certificate. Cointelegraph noted that the CS-SAF tokens contain metadata aligned with CORSIA.

Diesel R records follow the fuel across the supply chain

Across the second project, digital checkpoints collect Diesel R information at successive stages of production, transportation and use. Connecting those records would create a fuel history companies could consult when preparing emissions accounts. The Foundation places particular attention on Scope 3, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain, noting that the necessary information can sit in separate supplier, logistics and external systems.

Petrobras describes Diesel R as diesel containing a renewable portion produced by processing petroleum-based diesel alongside vegetable oils or animal fats. In the company’s explanation, the renewable material passes through refinery treatment involving hydrogen and catalysts. According to Petrobras’ product documentation, the resulting fuel can use existing engines, storage facilities and distribution infrastructure without adaptations, and the company sells Diesel R to fuel distributors that supply service stations in Brazil.

Why it matters

Fuel-related environmental claims are only as useful as they are verifiable, and both projects target the same weak point: the data trail behind a sustainability assertion. If a token cannot be reused or a batch cannot be quietly re-labelled, buyers and auditors gain a way to confirm that a claim still matches the fuel it describes.

The work also illustrates how state-linked energy producers are testing public blockchains for compliance-adjacent recordkeeping rather than for trading. For readers following Cardano, the significance is less about price and more about whether an enterprise-grade verification layer gains traction with large industrial counterparties.

Rafael Fraga, the Foundation’s Latin America business development lead, said the energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels. In the same statement, Fraga said increasingly complex supply chains make the origin, movement and reliability of environmental data important to the companies using it.

What to watch

Neither Crypto.news nor Cointelegraph reported a commercial launch date, so the next meaningful signal is whether the Cardano Foundation or Petrobras discloses fuel volumes, a scope expansion, or a timeline for broader deployment. A concurrent reference point is Shell’s Avelia Book-and-Claim platform, which the Cointelegraph report said had contributed to more than 84 million gallons of SAF entering the global fuel network since its 2022 launch, with over 780,000 tonnes of CO₂e abatement through June 2026.

The Cardano Foundation said the first is a sustainable aviation fuel application built on a Book-and-Claim model that tokenizes environmental attributes as CS-SAF tokens, and the second creates digital checkpoints that track production, transportation and use of Petrobras’ Diesel R renewable diesel, with attention to Scope 3 emissions reporting.

Under Book-and-Claim, the environmental benefit of sustainable aviation fuel can be separated from the physical fuel and assigned to an airline, company or passenger even when another operator uses the actual fuel. Petrobras’ aviation project records the origin and recipient of each allocation so a claim can be traced back to the underlying fuel certificate.

In the SAF case study, certificates are first checked against CORSIA and other recognized standards, then turned into standardized tokens carrying their environmental attributes. Participants can issue, transfer and inspect the tokens before retiring them when the benefit is claimed, and the Foundation describes that retirement step as preventing reuse.

What is Diesel R and how is it being tracked?

Petrobras describes Diesel R as diesel containing a renewable portion made by processing petroleum-based diesel alongside vegetable oils or animal fats. The Cardano Foundation’s project places digital checkpoints across production, transport and use to build a fuel history companies could consult when preparing emissions accounts.

When will Petrobras launch these Cardano applications commercially?

title: Unexpected package at your door? It could be a 'brushing scam' using your name for fake reviews
description:
If an unexpected package shows up at your door, it might seem harmless at first.
However, experts say it may actually indicate misuse of your personal data as part of a larger scam.
Unexpected packages are just one of several problems tied to online marketplaces and suspicious sellers.
• Online shoppers accused a company of misrepresenting its clothing and using AI after a sweater looked nothing like promised.
• Shoppers warned that mislabeled products on Amazon can slip through familiar listings.
text:
If an unexpected package shows up at your door, it might seem harmless at first. However, experts say it may actually indicate misuse of your personal data as part of a larger scam.

As the U.K. consumer advocacy organization Which? (@whichuk) said in an Instagram video, these unexplained deliveries often can be connected to efforts to game review systems and improve sellers' visibility on major shopping platforms.

Here's what to know

As the video explained, scams can start when a marketplace seller on sites like Amazon, eBay, or AliExpress obtains someone's personal details, probably from a data breach, and uses them to submit an order. Because the item is delivered, the platform identifies the transaction as a real purchase, which then allows the seller to post a fake favorable review in that victim's name.

Such scams are known as "brushing scams," according to Which?.

The consumer advocacy organization said sellers do this "at scale with cheap rubbish products" because the tactic is inexpensive while helping push those items higher in search results.

Which? said some of the surprise packages can come with a QR code and warned that scanning it might open a malicious site or trigger a malware download on the recipient's device.

What can be done?

Which? advised recipients to start by reporting the parcel to the platform on which the transaction took place. That way, the platform can be notified that the order may be linked to review manipulation.

People receiving mystery packages should also take steps to ensure that they have not been the victim of other kinds of identity theft. Such steps can include checking credit reports for unfamiliar accounts and using a data-breach lookup service to see whether any email addresses appear in a known leak.

Additionally, Which? urged viewers to "make sure all your online passwords are strong and unique. Or even better, use a password manager."

Where can I learn more?

Unexpected packages are just one of several problems tied to online marketplaces and suspicious sellers. These stories look at unsolicited deliveries, strange Amazon shipments, and products that did not match what shoppers expected.

• Across the U.S., officials warned that mysterious seed packages may carry invasive species risks.

• Residents were stunned when packages from overseas arrived unexpectedly, raising fears about hidden contaminants.

• An Amazon customer said a bizarre package from a seller prompted complaints.

• Online shoppers accused a company of misrepresenting its clothing and using AI after a sweater looked nothing like promised.

• Shoppers warned that mislabeled products on Amazon can slip through familiar listings.

Brazilian state-controlled oil company Petrobras has developed two blockchain applications using Cardano to track sustainability data for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and its Diesel R renewable fuel.

According to a Wednesday announcement from the Cardano Foundation, the first application, developed with PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs, tokenizes environmental attributes associated with SAF into digital tokens designed to prevent the same claim from being used more than once.

The application uses a Book-and-Claim model, which allows the environmental benefit to be separated from the physical fuel and assigned to an airline, company or passenger even if the SAF is used elsewhere.

Source: Cardano Foundation

The second application creates digital checkpoints to track the production, transportation and use of Diesel R, Petrobras’ renewable diesel fuel. The Cardano Foundation said the data could support Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain.

The projects are part of an ongoing research and development collaboration that began in 2023 with blockchain education for Petrobras employees and expanded in 2025 to energy-sector research with PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs. The Cardano Foundation did not disclose fuel volumes covered by the applications or a timeline for broader deployment.

Blockchain finds use in sustainable aviation fuel tracking

Shell has also used blockchain to track environmental attributes associated with sustainable aviation fuel through Avelia, a Book-and-Claim platform launched in 2022 that uses blockchain to track claims and prevent double counting.

In a September update, Shell said Avelia had contributed to more than 84 million gallons of SAF entering the global fuel network since its launch in 2022, resulting in more than 780,000 tonnes of CO₂e abatement through June 2026.

text:
Valmet, a leading global developer and supplier of process technologies, automation and services for the energy, pulp and paper industries, was selected by Strategic Biofuels to provide biomass power generation and flue gas cleaning technologies for its Louisiana Green Fuels (LGF) project in Caldwell Parish, Louisiana. The project is designed to integrate carbon-negative power generated from renewable forestry residuals with carbon capture and permanent geologic sequestration to produce deeply carbon-negative electric power.

Under its planned scope of work, Valmet will provide a boiler island featuring a circulating fluidized bed (CFB) boiler and advanced flue gas cleaning systems. The company’s unmatched large-scale proven biomass technologies are designed to support fuel flexibility, operational reliability and environmental performance while helping customers achieve ambitious sustainability objectives.

“Strategic Biofuels has cultivated strong partners for each area of this project to help ensure smooth and successful execution. By combining renewable power generation with carbon capture and sequestration, the project creates meaningful benefits for both the environment and the local community. Valmet’s expertise in biomass-fired boiler technology and flue gas cleaning supports the project’s goals for operational reliability, environmental performance, and long-term efficiency. We look forward to contributing to the project’s continued development,” says Lauri Pehu-Lehtonen, Vice President, Energy and Circularity, Valmet.

The LGF project is designed for more than 300 megawatts of gross generating capacity. At full buildout, the project is expected to annually consume more than 3.5 million tons of sustainably sourced forestry residuals, approximately 400 truckloads of biomass per day. The project’s post-combustion carbon capture and sequestration system is designed to capture and permanently store carbon dioxide in a fully permitted geologic reservoir.

title: This New Flight Booking Site Shows You the Climate Impact of Your Trip—and Lets You Pay ...
description:
For travelers who aren't willing or able to give up flying, there are ways to reduce the impact of individual trips.
New platforms like BookBetter are helping travelers not only do that research, but also make a tangible impact on reducing future CO2 emissions caused by aviation.
Travelers can compare routes and book flights directly on the platform, and have the option to purchase a contribution toward additional sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).
SAF is an alternative to conventional jet fuel that, depending on how it is produced, can substantially reduce lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions.
Of course, BookBetter isn't alone in trying to make flight emissions more visible when booking.
text:
Being able to fly to any place you wish, at any time you want, is an unbelievable feat of science and engineering. But that magic comes with a trade-off that's often all too easy to ignore.

For perspective, a transatlantic round-trip flight can generate roughly as much CO₂ per economy passenger as a typical American car emits in about two months, depending on the route and aircraft, according to calculations using data from the International Civil Aviation Organization and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Aviation is also responsible for close to four percent of observed, human-induced global warming to date, according to a 2021 study published in the journal Environmental Research Letters. And don't discount the effects of short-haul flights either. Data from the International Council on Clean Transportation shows that short domestic flights can be among the most carbon-intensive flights per mile, as much of the fuel is burned during takeoff and climb, before a plane reaches efficient cruising altitude.

For travelers who aren't willing or able to give up flying, there are ways to reduce the impact of individual trips. New platforms like BookBetter are helping travelers not only do that research, but also make a tangible impact on reducing future CO2 emissions caused by aviation.

BookBetter is a travel booking platform that gives users a clear picture of the environmental impact of their flight choices by outlining a route's contrail impact (aka, condensation trails that form at high altitudes and can trap heat) and carbon emissions per passenger. Travelers can compare routes and book flights directly on the platform, and have the option to purchase a contribution toward additional sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

SAF is an alternative to conventional jet fuel that, depending on how it is produced, can substantially reduce lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions. It isn't a zero-emissions solution: its climate benefit varies by feedstock and production method, supplies remain limited, and purchasing it through a book-and-claim system doesn't mean the fuel will power your specific flight. But advocates argue that creating additional demand can help scale a technology expected to play an important role in reducing aviation's reliance on fossil fuel.

SAF purchased on BookBetter doesn't specifically fuel the plane the traveler will fly on (it isn't available at every airport), but customers who purchase it do get a certificate that lists a unique ID, the name of the SAF producer, the airport it was delivered to, the volume of emissions reduced, and more, giving travelers as much transparency into their contribution as possible.

"Nicolas Guillaume and I spent years working on alternative fuel for aviation and night trains, watching technical solutions pile up while the actual products for travelers stayed stuck in the past," Louis Lammertyn, co-founder of BookBetter, told Travel + Leisure, about the inspiration behind the platform. "BookBetter exists because the tools to fly better already exist today. They just weren't connected to the traveler who could actually use them."

Lammertyn explained they consciously chose SAF over carbon credits because they believe going directly to the source (aka, the fuel) is "really helping the aviation industry transform." He noted that this way, you're physically replacing "fossil kerosene in the fuel system, rather than funding a distant project to compensate by planting trees, while the aviation industry keeps emitting and does not transform. When you book with BookBetter, your contribution to cleaner skies is certified, traceable, and named, not a feel-good rounding error at checkout."

Of course, BookBetter isn't alone in trying to make flight emissions more visible when booking. Google Flights has displayed a carbon estimate next to nearly every fare since 2021, with a filter to show only lower-emissions alternatives. Skyscanner also offers a similar filter. However, neither lets you actually purchase SAF. Price is also part of BookBetter's ranking algorithm, so lower-emission options don't necessarily mean choosing the most expensive flight.

"BookBetter ranks flights by combining emissions and price in a single algorithm, so the option that rises to the top is a genuinely better value in every sense," Lammertyn explained. In practice, that means the platform tends to favor routes and flight options that are already cheaper, with a direct flight on a newer aircraft in economy (which also happens to be the cleaner option) usually costing less than a connection in business class.

But Lammertyn is clear on the fact that none of this adds up to a perfect solution.

"We do not want to call it fully sustainable, since even on 100 percent SAF, a flight would still have a negative climate effect of around 20 percent of the fossil CO2 it emits today," he said, pointing to non-CO2 warming effects as an additional factor they cannot control. If you really want the most sustainable travel choice, his advice is to take a train. (BookBetter has a rail tab on its site to help you with that, too.) But when you have to fly, make it count.

According to Lammertyn, more than 30,000 people have tested BookBetter to date, including travelers who don't necessarily consider sustainability their primary concern.

"The traveler the industry keeps calling niche, the one who wants to go far, go well, and leave the smallest mark possible, turns out to be far more common than anyone admitted," he said. "You do not have to stop exploring the world. You just deserve a platform that helps you do it better."

title: Latin America SAF Gap Drives Corporate Scope 3 Demand Pooling
description:
Latin America's transition to sustainable aviation fuel faces a structural bottleneck due to zero commercial-scale refining capacity despite abundant regional feedstocks.
To overcome high SAF green premiums and meet CORSIA mandates, carriers like Aeroméxico are partnering with corporate giants to pool Scope 1 and Scope 3 emissions reductions.
Currently, SAF accounts for just 1.6% of the carrier's fuel mix, reflecting a broader structural bottleneck across Latin America, where commercial-scale SAF refining capacity remains non-existent.
The absence of regional SAF refining capacity leaves Latin American airlines vulnerable to rising compliance costs.
Mexico's pathway toward sustainable aviation fuel illustrates the broader economic challenges facing emerging markets during the global energy transition.
text:
Latin America's transition to sustainable aviation fuel faces a structural bottleneck due to zero commercial-scale refining capacity despite abundant regional feedstocks. To overcome high SAF green premiums and meet CORSIA mandates, carriers like Aeroméxico are partnering with corporate giants to pool Scope 1 and Scope 3 emissions reductions. This development impacts airlines, energy firms, multinational exporters, and air cargo logistics across Mexico's nearshoring corridors.

——

Global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production is projected to reach 2.4 million tons in 2026, accounting for 0.8% of worldwide jet fuel consumption and representing an annual procurement cost of US$4.3 billion for commercial carriers. Despite its current scarcity, SAF stands as the primary technical lever for decarbonizing civil aviation, offering up to an 80% reduction in lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared to conventional petroleum-based jet fuel. However, achieving the global airline industry's net-zero carbon commitment by 2050 requires annual SAF production to scale to 500 million tonnes — a 200-fold expansion that demands unprecedented capital deployment across raw material supply chains, refining infrastructure, and green financing mechanisms.

In Mexico, flag carrier Aeroméxico has mapped a long-term decarbonization pathway where SAF must constitute 63% of total fuel burn by 2050. Currently, SAF accounts for just 1.6% of the carrier's fuel mix, reflecting a broader structural bottleneck across Latin America, where commercial-scale SAF refining capacity remains non-existent. To bridge this supply gap and stimulate domestic demand, Aeroméxico partnered with Grupo Bimbo and Compartamos Banco, launching Latin America's first corporate travel program designed to co-fund SAF procurement by linking the airline's Scope 1 operational emissions reductions with corporate partners' Scope 3 business travel accounting.

Latin America's transition to sustainable aviation fuel is trapped in a structural paradox: while the region possesses world-class agricultural and industrial waste feedstocks, the total absence of domestic commercial refining infrastructure forces regional airlines to face prohibitive green premiums or export raw materials abroad. Consequently, voluntary corporate Scope 3 demand pooling across passenger travel and nearshoring air cargo supply chains will serve as the primary engine for regional market liquidity until industrial refining assets and statutory frameworks align under international mandates like CORSIA.

The Raw Material Paradox: Biomass Wealth vs. Refining Vacuum

Latin America holds one of the world's most abundant biomass reserve profiles, generating millions of tons of agricultural residue, sugarcane ethanol, used cooking oil (UCO), and animal tallow annually. Per World Economic Forum data, global feedstock availability is sufficient to cover regional decarbonization requirements toward 2050.

However, this biological wealth contrasts sharply with a complete absence of domestic commercial refining infrastructure. Processing raw biomass into drop-in synthetic paraffinic kerosene (SPK) requires advanced refining pathways, such as Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) or Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) technology. Currently, Mexico possesses zero operational commercial-scale SAF plants. While federal authorities have initiated exploratory discussions with international energy partners to evaluate technology sharing, state energy company PEMEX remains constrained by financial debt and capital commitments to conventional oil refining at the Olmeca facility in Dos Bocas.

This infrastructure deficit creates a severe market inefficiency. Without local processing facilities, Mexican feedstock collection networks export unrefined waste oils and tallow to processing hubs in the United States and Europe, where policy mechanisms — such as the US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) clean fuel production tax credits — subsidize refining margins. Mexican carriers seeking to procure certified SAF must subsequently import finished fuel at steep international logistics costs, paying a green premium two to four times higher than standard Jet-A.

Scope 3 Demand Pooling Across Travel and Cargo Supply Chains

In developed aviation markets, regulatory mandates and direct government subsidies accelerate SAF adoption. The European Union's ReFuelEU Aviation regulation enforces blending mandates starting at 2% in 2025 and scaling to 70% by 2050. In contrast, Mexico and broader Latin America operate in a policy environment lacking direct financial subsidies or enforceable blending quotas. To overcome the green premium without jeopardizing operating margins, airlines are developing corporate co-funding models.

The corporate alliance established between Aeroméxico, Grupo Bimbo, and Compartamos Banco provides a commercial blueprint for emerging markets. Under this framework, corporate clients commit capital to purchase SAF environmental attributes tied to employee business travel. Aeroméxico claims direct Scope 1 operational emissions reductions under civil aviation reporting, while corporate partners claim verified Scope 3 carbon reductions across their value chains.

This demand-pooling mechanism addresses the fundamental liquidity barrier facing regional SAF deployment. According to the Air Transport Action Group, scaling global SAF production requires up to US$1.5 trillion in cumulative capital investment for 5,000 to 7,000 production facilities worldwide. Co-funding models mitigate price volatility by sharing the green premium across major corporate energy consumers.

CORSIA Compliance, Global Benchmarks, and Regulatory Exposures

As international climate regulations tighten, Latin American carriers face escalating financial risks under ICAO's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Under ICAO CORSIA Phase 1 (2024–2026), baseline requirements are set at 85% of 2019 levels, creating mandatory offsetting obligations for international flights between participating states. In official regulatory filings, Aeroméxico submitted CORSIA emissions compliance reports to Mexico's Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC).

The absence of regional SAF refining capacity leaves Latin American airlines vulnerable to rising compliance costs. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) warned that green compliance costs and fleet delivery constraints will compress airline profit margins globally through 2026. For Latin American carriers operating in price-sensitive consumer markets, relying exclusively on carbon credit offsets rather than physical SAF blending exposes balance sheets to carbon market price volatility.

International benchmarks illustrate the competitive gap between global carriers and Latin American operators. According to corporate sustainability disclosures, KLM reached a 4.6% SAF share in its global fuel mix in 2025, while International Airlines Group (IAG) utilized over 291,000 tonnes of SAF (3.3% of its total fuel burn), Lufthansa Group achieved 1.5%, and United Airlines recorded approximately 0.7%. Without local refining capacity, Latin American carriers risk falling behind global peers as CORSIA compliance rules become more stringent.

Capital Allocation and the 2050 Decarbonization Equation

To achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, commercial airlines must balance fleet modernizations with alternative fuel adoption. While modern aircraft inductions yield immediate fuel efficiency gains, fleet replacement alone cannot bridge the long-term decarbonization deficit. In its annual ESG disclosures, Aeroméxico reported a 10% emissions reduction compared to pre-pandemic baselines through Boeing 737 MAX and 787 Dreamliner inductions.

However, aeronautical engineering constraints dictate that thermodynamic fleet efficiency improvements hit a structural ceiling once young aircraft integration stabilizes, leaving SAF blending to deliver 63% of Aeroméxico's required emissions reductions by 2050.

This transition imposes severe capital requirements across a sector navigating tight financial margins. While global airline profitability maintains steady baseline performance — with IATA having projected global industry net profits of US$41 billion in 2026 on revenues of US$1.053 trillion — Latin American carriers operate under narrower net profit margins and elevated foreign exchange volatility. Passing green premiums directly onto passenger fares risks depressing traffic, making corporate co-funding, domestic refining investments, and public-private risk-sharing mechanisms essential to securing Mexico's role as a competitive, low-carbon hub for global trade and transport.

Mexico's pathway toward sustainable aviation fuel illustrates the broader economic challenges facing emerging markets during the global energy transition. While feedstock abundance provides a strong foundational advantage, converting biological resources into commercial aviation decarbonization requires bridging the industrial refining gap and establishing permanent capital-sharing mechanisms. By leveraging corporate Scope 3 partnerships, advancing regional trade alignment under USMCA, and structuring public policy around bio-energy investment, Mexico can secure its position as a competitive, low-carbon hub for global trade and transport.

text:
The scope of the commercial agreement between Plug Power and Arcadia eFuels – the Danish start-up, which has, however, relocated its headquarters to Austin, Texas – has been significantly expanded. The company specialises in the construction of plants for the production of synthetic aviation fuels, known as eSAFs.

As announced by the US company, the parties have in fact signed a new agreement – following the one signed in 2023 regarding the plant to be built at the port of Vordingborg in Denmark – which designates Plug as the preferred supplier of PEM electrolysers for a further four plants that the Scandinavian group intends to develop across Europe and the Americas.

According to the statement, the total electrolysis capacity would amount to over 1 GW and would be in addition to the 280 MW planned for the Danish project, known as ENDOR, for which the completion timeline has since been extended beyond the 2023 forecast. The FID was scheduled for 2024, whilst production was expected to commence in 2026.

The new press release does not specify an updated deadline for the final investment decision and states that deliveries of the electrolysers will commence following formal authorisation to proceed.

In the meantime, Arcadia has nevertheless found a buyer for part of its future output. The German energy group Uniper, in fact, has committed to purchasing 40,000 tonnes of e-SAF per year from the Danish plant. The contract covers a period of more than 10 years and provides for deliveries to begin in the early years of the next decade.

Once completed, the Vordingborg plant will use electricity generated from wind power to produce, via Plug’s electrolysis system, around 110 tonnes of green hydrogen per day. The H2 it will then be combined with CO2 captured to produce eSAF.

“The agreement extends our collaboration with Arcadia eFuels from ENDOR to other plants that will be built in Europe and the Americas in the future, confirming confidence in our technology and our ability to deliver projects of this scale,” commented José Luis Crespo, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Plug. “European aviation fuel mandates are driving demand for e-SAFs. Producing them using electricity and CO2 ”of European origin also helps to strengthen the continent’s energy security by reducing dependence on imported oil’.

“The contract with Plug is one of the agreements already finalised as part of the process leading up to the final investment decision for ENDOR,” added Amy Hebert, Chief Executive of Arcadia eFuels. “To achieve aviation’s decarbonisation targets, we will need fuels produced from renewable hydrogen and captured CO₂. Plug has the experience and supply capacity required for our plant, as well as the reliability demanded by our financiers.”.

title: Vertical Aerospace has already started work on its hybrid-electric demonstrator
description:
Now, the same Vertical Aerospace VX4 prototype sits dismantled inside a hangar at Cotswold Airport, preparing for a second life.
Key to this is the integration of a secondary fuel system, and for G-EVTA, this means removing several battery packs to make way for a gas turbine, generator and fuel system.
Vertical hopes to begin flight testing with the hybrid electric demonstrator early in 2027.
Airport availability also complicated the proposed return flight, making road transport the more practical way to get the hybrid work started.
These are development targets for the future hybrid aircraft rather than capabilities already demonstrated by AC2.
text:
Two months ago, it was flying in front of thousands of people at Farnborough Airshow. Now, the same Vertical Aerospace VX4 prototype sits dismantled inside a hangar at Cotswold Airport, preparing for a second life.

During AGN’s visit to the opening of the first production facility for Vertical’s groundbreaking Valo passenger aircraft, engineers explained how they are converting this VX4 prototype into a hybrid-electric demonstrator.

While Vertical’s core work on building the first Valo continues, the company is looking to move beyond short, fully electric passenger flights into longer-range cargo, commercial and defence operations. Key to this is the integration of a secondary fuel system, and for G-EVTA, this means removing several battery packs to make way for a gas turbine, generator and fuel system.

At the back of the company’s newly opened Aircraft Assembly Centre, the aircraft known internally as AC2 offered a very different sight from its Farnborough flying display. Its disassembled state was evidence of the next phase already getting under way.

Vertical hopes to begin flight testing with the hybrid electric demonstrator early in 2027.

Why Vertical’s Farnborough aircraft came home by road

AC2 had completed close to 90 flights, according to production manager Ellis, including numerous full piloted transitions that prepared it to fly repeatedly at Farnborough.

Its newer counterpart, Aircraft Three, is now continuing the all-electric flight-test campaign. That frees the earlier aircraft for conversion while Vertical keeps gathering flight data.

Despite having demonstrated its capabilities in the air, AC2 returned from Farnborough by road. The team explained that preparing Aircraft Three for its flight campaign had taken priority. Airport availability also complicated the proposed return flight, making road transport the more practical way to get the hybrid work started.

“We wanted to start [the] hybrid programme sooner,” Ellis said.

Dismantling the aircraft for transport also fit the work that awaited it at Kemble. Rather than get it all prepared for a ferry flight only to then take it apart again, the team could proceed towards the modification before AC2 even left Farnborough.

The aircraft took around three or four days to break down into subassemblies. When AGN visited, the team was inspecting its components ahead of the conversion.

How the VX4 is becoming a hybrid-electric aircraft

The biggest change will be how the aircraft obtains its electrical energy.

The conversion removes four of its eight battery packs. A gas turbine and generator will be installed within the fuselage, with a fuel tank behind them, while the remaining batteries continue to form part of the power system.

The propellers will still be driven by electric motors. The turbine’s role is to generate electricity, rather than mechanically turn the propellers.

“The batteries, the HV cables to the motors remain the same,” Ellis explained. “That whole architecture is exactly the same as it was.”

Some existing structure will be removed and new structure installed to support the engine. The team will also receive additional training for working with the fuel system.

Asked whether the integration presented any particularly daunting challenges, Ellis was relaxed about the work ahead. The technicians already have experience building and modifying Vertical’s prototypes, while a complete hybrid powertrain is being tested separately on the ground.

One detail remained firmly under wraps. When AGN asked who was supplying the turbine, the answer was brief: “Wait and see.”

Ground testing prepares the hybrid for flight

Although the dismantled aircraft makes the programme newly tangible, Vertical has been developing its hybrid technology for several years.

The company announced the programme in May 2025. A year later, it reported that integration testing had begun on its Hybrid Propulsion Evaluation Rig, known as HYPER, following more than two years of development.

The rig allows engineers to test the turbine, generator, electrical systems and controls together, including how they respond to faults, before installing the system in an aircraft.

Vertical has described the turbine as compatible with sustainable aviation fuel. The hybrid will nevertheless burn fuel, bringing a different operating and emissions profile from the fully electric Valo.

During the tour, the team said the work now centres on fitting that tested system into the prototype, including the structural changes needed for the installation.

Why Vertical wants greater range and payload

Vertical’s ambitions for the eventual hybrid variant are considerably greater than those of its electric passenger aircraft.

The company is targeting a range of up to 1,000 miles – approximately 870 nm – and configurations carrying up to 1,100 kg. These are development targets for the future hybrid aircraft rather than capabilities already demonstrated by AC2.

For Stuart Simpson, Vertical’s CEO, that additional capability creates opportunities beyond the short journeys envisaged for the all-electric Valo.

“The hybrid then opens up new opportunities with increased range, and it also opens it up for military opportunities for distributed logistics, where they want to be able to carry a much higher payload,” he said.

The aim is to serve more markets using shared aircraft technology. Electric passenger services, longer commercial journeys and military resupply have different requirements, but Vertical believes variants of its platform can address them without starting each design from scratch.

The fully electric aircraft remains the immediate certification priority. All seven Valos planned for the initial certification programme will be electric, with UK type certification targeted for 2029. The hybrid demonstrator’s planned flights in the first half of 2027 will support a separate development effort.

For AC2, the next public appearance could therefore look familiar while concealing a substantial change inside. The aircraft that helped demonstrate electric transition flight at Farnborough is now being rebuilt to explore how far that technology can travel with a turbine aboard.

text:
After more than a century in business, Coast Packing is finding that what’s old is new again.

On a recent episode of The Food Institute Podcast, guest host Justin D’Affronte of City National Bank spoke with Coast Packing chairman and CEO Eric Gustafson about the company’s 104 year family legacy, renewed consumer interest in lard and beef tallow, and the economic pressures facing food manufacturers in California.

Founded by Gustafson’s great-grandfather and his business partner in 1922, Coast Packing began as a full-line slaughter and meatpacking facility in Vernon, California. When changing economics led the company to exit slaughter operations in the 1960s, it pivoted toward products it had previously produced as byproducts: lard and tallow.

That decision ultimately established Coast Packing’s modern identity as a specialist in animal fat shortenings.

Today, Gustafson represents the fourth generation of his family to lead the business.

“I’m very fortunate and blessed to be the fourth-generation CEO and chairman,” Gustafson said. “Certainly didn’t come easy and still isn’t, but I feel very fortunate [and] honored that I’m trusted by my family and my employees to lead this business forward.”

Animal Fats Come Full Circle

One of the biggest changes Gustafson has witnessed during his 16-plus years as CEO is a shift in how consumers perceive animal fats.

After decades in which lard, tallow, and saturated fats faced scrutiny, he feels consumers have become increasingly interested in natural and minimally processed ingredients. That movement has helped generate new interest in Coast Packing’s core products.

“It’s fun to see things come full circle with these consumer trends that are supporting our business again,” Gustafson said. Lard and tallow serve different culinary purposes.

Lard, which comes from pork fat, remains prominent in applications such as tamales, flour tortillas, baked goods and pie crusts. Tallow, derived from beef fat, is particularly suited to heavy-duty frying.

Gustafson pointed to growing restaurant interest in beef tallow for French fries, arguing that it can offer advantages in taste, texture and operational performance.

For foodservice operators, he said tallow can also provide longer fry life and require less cleaning than some alternatives. Coast Packing generally sees customers achieve at least a 50% reduction in frying-oil usage when switching to tallow, according to Gustafson.

California Manufacturing Challenges

While Coast Packing remains deeply rooted in Southern California, Gustafson expressed concern about the difficulty of operating a manufacturing business in the state.

“I love California, born and raised,” he said, but added that its regulatory environment has “made it more challenging to operate here as a manufacturer.”

Those challenges extend to sourcing. While Coast Packing continues to work with suppliers in Central California, Gustafson said the majority of its raw materials now come from the Midwest and other parts of the country.

He argued that higher regulatory and operating costs ultimately reach consumers, either through the price of locally manufactured goods or the expense associated with transporting products into California from elsewhere.

Labor presents another challenge – and responsibility. Gustafson emphasized that Coast Packing’s longevity depends on building a culture in which employees and the business succeed together.

“If there’s no employees, there’s no Coast Packing,” he said. “But without Coast Packing, you won’t have employees.”

Commodity Markets Add Pressure

Beyond regulation and labor, Coast Packing must navigate volatile commodity markets.

Gustafson explained that food producers increasingly compete for fats and oils with renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel manufacturers. Changes in crude-oil markets and government incentives for renewable fuels can therefore ripple into the price of edible fats.

At the same time, tight U.S. cattle supplies put additional pressure on the tallow market. With fewer animals available and multiple industries competing for raw materials, basic supply-and demand dynamics can quickly push costs higher.

Despite those pressures, Coast Packing is looking to capitalize on renewed interest in its century-old product categories. The company’s website now offers recipes, educational resources, “Taste Maps” identifying restaurants and bakeries that use lard and tallow, and a beef tallow savings calculator for foodservice operators.

For a company founded in 1922, changing consumer tastes may ultimately be bringing Coast Packing back to where it started: making traditional ingredients relevant to a new generation.

description:

text:
Brazil's state-controlled oil company is turning to blockchain technology to bring more accountability to the market for lower-carbon fuels. Petrobras has developed two research applications on the Cardano network to track environmental claims tied to sustainable aviation fuel and its partly renewable diesel product, the Cardano Foundation announced Wednesday.

The projects, built in partnership with Ledger Labs at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio), aim to solve a structural problem in how green fuel attributes are bought and sold. One application, called CS-SAF, tokenizes the environmental benefits of certified jet fuel. The other creates digital checkpoints to trace the journey of Diesel R, Petrobras' renewable diesel, from production through consumption.

"Brazil has been one of the most consistent adopters of Cardano, from SERPRO in government to SENAI in industry," said Frederik Gregaard, chief executive of the Cardano Foundation. "It's great to see Petrobras, one of the largest firms in the region, continue to see value in on-chain provenance and traceability."

The aviation project addresses a specific weakness in the sustainable fuel market. Under what is known as a book-and-claim model, an airline can pay for the environmental benefit of sustainable aviation fuel even when the physical product is delivered elsewhere. That separation creates an accounting challenge: without a reliable registry, two different companies could potentially claim the same emissions reduction.

CS-SAF attempts to close that gap by issuing digital tokens on Cardano that represent certified sustainability attributes. Before any token is minted, the platform verifies that the underlying fuel meets the requirements of CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation established by the International Civil Aviation Organization. Once a buyer makes a claim, the corresponding token is permanently retired on-chain, preventing reuse.

The system also includes a passenger-facing application. Travelers can enter their departure and destination airports, calculate the fuel benefit associated with their journey, and receive a digital certificate linking their allocation back to the original fuel certificate. Petrobras produces its sustainable aviation fuel at the Duque de Caxias refinery through co-processing petroleum inputs with renewable materials.

The second application takes a different approach, focusing on traceability rather than claim management. It would record information at each stage of Diesel R's production, transportation and use, assembling those records into a complete history of the fuel's journey. The Cardano Foundation said such data could support Scope 3 emissions reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company's value chain — information that often resides with suppliers and customers rather than the reporting company itself.

Petrobras markets Diesel R in versions with different renewable content, including R5 at 5% and R10 at 10%. The varying renewable shares underscore why precise records matter: a fuel's renewable content, its calculated lifecycle emissions, and the benefit a buyer may report are distinct pieces of information that auditors need to verify independently.

Both projects remain firmly in the research phase. The diesel model is described as proposed, and the announcement disclosed neither the fuel volumes covered by the applications nor a timeline for broader deployment. The public case study also does not identify participating airline customers or report how many sustainability claims have been retired through the system.

Certification remains the governing authority for sustainable fuel claims. Petrobras' aviation fuel has received CORSIA sustainability certification through recognized frameworks, which require detailed evidence of feedstocks, production methods, and lifecycle carbon emissions. A blockchain record can help trace a certificate after it is issued, but it does not replace the comprehensive certification process required for regulatory compliance.

"Institutional interest in Cardano keeps growing, especially with x402 arriving on Cardano and Fireblocks adding support for Cardano Native Tokens," Gregaard added. "It's never been a better time for enterprises to consider what this technology offers."

The collaboration between Petrobras and the Cardano Foundation began in 2023 with blockchain education for the energy company's employees. It expanded in 2025 to include energy-sector research with PUC-Rio's Ledger Labs.

Petrobras is not alone in exploring blockchain for sustainable fuel accounting. Shell launched Avelia, a book-and-claim platform, in 2022. In a September update, the energy major said Avelia had contributed to more than 84 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel entering the global fuel network since its launch, resulting in more than 780,000 tonnes of CO2e abatement through June 2026. Australia's Viva Energy signed an agreement with NoviqTech in January to research digital book-and-claim systems for sustainable aviation fuel.

The practical measure of success for Petrobras' initiative will be whether the system makes certificate reconciliation faster, gives auditors sufficient evidence, and interoperates with other registries. Documented results on those points would strengthen the case for adopting blockchain-based tracking across the broader fuel supply chain. For now, the projects represent a notable test of whether distributed ledger technology can bring greater transparency to the increasingly complex market for lower-carbon fuels.

text:
Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled energy company, has built two research-stage blockchain applications on Cardano to record the environmental claims tied to its sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel, the Cardano Foundation announced on Wednesday.

Both came out of a research and development partnership between Petrobras, the Swiss not-for-profit Cardano Foundation and Rio de Janeiro’s Pontifical Catholic University (PUC-Rio). The goal is to make emissions and fuel lifecycle data easier to check, as airlines and passengers look for ways to verify green fuel claims.

Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.

One Credit, One Claim

The first tool covers sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), a lower-carbon jet fuel that works in existing aircraft and airport infrastructure. It runs on a Book-and-Claim model, which splits the fuel’s environmental benefit from the physical fuel so that the benefit can be credited to an airline, company or traveler even if the fuel was produced or used somewhere else.

According to the foundation’s case study, each SAF attribute is issued on Cardano as a standardized token called CS-SAF, with metadata aligned to CORSIA, the carbon offsetting scheme for international aviation. The tokens can be minted, transferred and retired, which is meant to stop the same benefit from being counted twice.

Passengers can type in their departure and arrival airports, work out the matching CS-SAF amount and receive a certificate showing their route, distance and allocation, linked to the original fuel certificate.

Tracking Diesel R

The second tool targets Diesel R, Petrobras’ renewable diesel brand, and was built with PUC-Rio. The foundation described it as a proposed model that logs checkpoints as the fuel is produced, transported and used, building a single record of its lifecycle.

That record is aimed at Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain and often depends on data held by suppliers and logistics firms.

“The energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels,” said Rafael Fraga, LATAM business development lead at the Cardano Foundation. “Public blockchain gives us the opportunity to make that trust part of the system by design.”

The announcement did not give a timeline for commercial rollout of either tool.

From Training to Traceability

The work extends a relationship that started in December 2023, when the Cardano Foundation agreed to run blockchain education workshops for Petrobras staff through Petrobras University, a program open to more than 40,000 employees. In April 2025, the foundation announced a research collaboration with PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs that would focus first on blockchain uses for renewable fuels, with Petrobras as an industry partner.

title: US scientists develop catalyst to turn woody biomass into jet fuel components
description:
